After the usual preliminaries on such an occasion were gone through, His Excellency Governor Feddersen addressed the company in Danish, in words to the following effect: "Gentlemen þÿ The Government of these Islands will be delivered over to-morrow to my successor, 1 .jvernor Schlesel. In a few days I will leave this Island. I recommend myself to your friendly remembrance." His Excellency, who seemed deeply impressed at these words, then was and retired. The company bowed all attention 5 but Ilis Excellency Governor Schlesel bowed and retired also. The Levee being over Their Excellencies repaired to the Parade Ground in front of the Fort, where the Military was drawn up, under command of Baron Rosenkrantz. Ilis Excellency Governor Fcdd>rsen , in presenting Governor Schlegtl , addressed them thus : Soldiers ; I present to you His " Excellency Governor Schlegel who , has been appointed by His Majesty the King Governor of these Islands and over you. I thank you for the endurance and faithfulness which you have manifested under every circumstance. I leave you. I feel confident that you will fulfill your duties under the command of His Excellency Governor Schlegel, as you have done then command." The Military under my formed into platoons and marched to the Barrack. Before closing these remarks, and in consequence of His Excellency Gover-

From the N. Y. Journal of Commerce, Mar. 30. LATE FRO.fi HAVANA

The steamship Philadelphia, Captain Schenck, reached this port last night, bringing news from Havana to noon of the 23rd instant. The papers published on the day of the steamer's departure give full accounts of the execution of the unfortunate Don Ramon Pinto, formerly a friend of General Concha, who was arrested on the morning of the 6th of February, after a hall at the Palace of the Governor General himself, at which it is pretended his assassination was to have taken place, and a revolution initiated. We translate the account of the execution, as given by the Prensa de la Hahana, which takes the occasion to moralize editorially against all endeavors to wrest "from Spain the fair possession in the new world, which was discovered for that country by the fleets of Isabella the Catholic." "Don Ramon Pinto, who was sentenced on the 10th instant, in a Council of war held by the permanent military Commission of this Island to the ignominious death of the garote, for the crime of conspiracy against the State, was on Wednesday last, at 7 A. M., removed from the Castle de la Punta to the Royal Prison, where he was placed in the Chapel of the Condemned, there to remain until the same hour of the ensuing day, which had been fixed upon for l»is execution. At the earliest dawn of Thursday morning, immense crowds were already pouring from every avenue which leads to the principal front of the prison ; and the neighboring walls, the top of the Castle itself, and the windows

and roofsof the neighboring houses were densely tilled with people curious to witness the coming scene. The platform of the garote was placed in the centre of the spacious place de la Punta , on the same spot on which it had been set up for Don Narciso Lopez, and a little after six o'clock the executioner took his place upon the fatal machine, whilst the multitude encompassed it still more closely on every side. At half after six, the troops, composed of a small detachment from each portion of the army þÿ from the infantry, cavalry, volunteers, and municipal guard þÿ began to form into a square around the scaffold. At 7 o'clock the senior officer of the place made the customary proclamation, repeating it three times. A moment later, the agitation of the crowd showed that the criminal had departed from the prison. From the prison doors to the square of soldiery, a long narrow lane was now formed, each side of which was composed of the silent, immovable multitude. Through this terrible lane there soon appeared, first the Holy Brother-

hood of Peace and Charity, with their banners, and then a solid square of twenty in fully diers, the midst of whom walked the armed and accoutred solcondemned Pinto, surrounded by priests, bearing a crucifix clasped in his hands, and followed by the doomsman who was to perform the work of justice. The criminal was dressed in drill ashcolored pantaloons, with a fine black stripe; low patent leather shoes, without buckles or straps; white stockings; a lilac-colored ground drill frock coat, with large black plaid pattern; and over this the loug white garment worn by those to be executed, which was bound with a white silk cincture round the waist, but sufficiently open at the top for the coat to he visible. On his head he wore the usual white night cap, having a small black cross on that part of it which falls over the forehead. lie was conducted slowly, to the sound of the drum, from the prison to the scaffold, and listened, meanwhile, with serenity to the exhortations of the clergyman who assisted him. He appeared perfectly calm and self-possessed until lie came in sight of the instruments of death ; but here he was evidently much moved, and lost, in a measure, his firmness of step, though not sufficiently to require aid in walking. At the foot of the step of the platform on which the garote stood, he gave his right hand to the priest who accompanied him, and his left to the executioner, that they might assist him to ascend. On the scaffold, he listened attentively to the

last exhortations of the minister of God, said a few words in a low tone, which could only he heard by Him to whom they were directed, placed himself on the fatal seat, commenced a last prayer, and his soul fled to the presence of his Divine Creator. 'Don Ramon Pinto had ceased to exist.' During the whole awful scene, and the solemn preparations for death which preceded it, the most perfect silence was preserved by the spectators. All was still, as though the execution had taken place in a church. Not a sound, not a voice, not a cry, and not a sign of applause was manifested either before or afterwards, þÿ revealing how entirely prudence, judgment and civilization prevail, and how terrible the impression produced by what took place, on all who were present." IIow far the unfortunate man, an account of whose last hours is thus briefly given, merited the terrible doom which has befallen him, it is perhaps not possible as yet to determine. The course of General Concha has certainly been severe in the extreme, if not cruel, and the stern, vindictive policy which Lis measures have exhibited during the year, since his return from Spain, has done more to alienate the affections of Cuba from the mother country, than could have been accomplished by fili bustering pirates in half a century. Nevertheless, the death of Pinto may not be laid entirely at his door. Americans who have encouraged Cubans to rebellion, by lying hopes of assistance from this country; Annexationists and out-

rage manufacturers who have, for years past, carefully fanned each spark out of which a flame of international discord might he created, have laid the foundation for the deep-seated, justifiable jealousy which prevails among Cuban authorities, and whatever their guilt trtay be, let us before raising a cry of horror, remember how far we have made ourselvcs participators in their crime.

From the Barbados Globe, April. 12 We extract the following article on the completion of the Panama Railroad from the Morning Journal of the 20th ultimo : þÿ One of the greatest and most promising undertakings of the age has at length been brought to a successful issue. 1 he Panama Railroad connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, has been completed and opened, across and trains are now the Isthmus from regularly running The existence sea to sea. of this road is owing solely to American enterprise, energy, and capital ; it is to the citizens of the United States that the world is indebted for the successful edly completion of to a work destined exert which is undoubt- a most beneficial and widely-extended influence upon the commerce of nations. The Panama Railroad Company was organized under a grant from New Granada of the lands through which the line passes for a period of 49 years (firing which time no other road of any kind can be built without the previous consent of the Company, þÿ and also under a charter from the State of New-York. After careful preliminary surveys, operations were fairly commenced in 1850, and by the end of the year 1854 the road was finished. Since the year 1852, however, certain portions of" the line, as they were completed, have been used for the transpor- þÿ tation of passengers and light freight, for some months past indeed no fewer than 38 miles have been in successful working. The entire road extends from the port of Navy Bay on the Atlantic to the Bay of Panama on the Pacific, its

whole length being about 49 miles. "Its guage is five feet; its grades easy, the highest for a short distance near the summit being 00 feet to the mile on the Pacific and 53 feet to the mile on the Atlantic slope; the summit being only 250 feet above the level of the sea. It is well built, and in the opinion of engineers who have reported upon it, is in every respect as good a road as any on the Continent of America. Some of the bridges are of iron, and it is intended to replace all the wooden structures with that material. The neutrality of the Isthmus it traverses is guaranteed by the Government of the United States by

also by Great Britain and the United States by what is known as the Bulwer of nations." The road promises to be a Treaty. It thus becomes the highway der the fostering care of the late lamentprofitable concern, and amply to remunerate those who undertook to lay it down. "The revenue of that portion of the line hitherto used, notwithstanding the expensive mule carriage from its terminus to Panama, has been sufficient to pay all running expenses, and leave an ample surplus to pay interest on its bonds and dividends on its stock, averaging ovei one per cent., per annum. This revenue had been derived from a single train each way daily þÿ six trains in the week. The average receipts have heen more than eighteen dollars, or upwards of 2 1. 10s. per mile for every mile a train has been run, being more than ten times the average receipts on the best roads in the United States or Europe. With such receipts the proportion of expense to income is much less than on any other road in the world; and when in full operation it is supposed that one-fifth of its gross income will be sufficient to pay all its expenses without
across the Isthmus beyond the average of the last three years. The. increased rates of charge for thorough transit will yield a net revenue of fully 15 per cent

3 þÿ Ifc <3> ¬ 1 32L iiTlS, on its entire cost, whilst the charge to passengers will then be only about one half, and for merchandize one fifth of the former expense of mule carriage." A road that will pay as well as this is not at all likely to prove a failure, and the advantages it affords of cheap and easy transit from ocean to ocean cannot fail soon to make it a great highway of commerce. It is impossible indeed to form anything like an adequate estimate of the benefits that this enterprise promises to confer upon the world. It will entirely divert navigation from its ancient paths, and bring nations hitherto separated from each other by a distance of more than half the circumference of the globe within easy access of one another, to their mutual advantage, and to the general good of mankind. There is every likelihood of the Panama route becoming par excellence, the highway of the world's commerce; that the dangerous navigation of the "Cape of storms" will in time be entirely abandoned, the manufactories of Europe conveyed by way of the Isthmus to the whole western side of America, from Behring's Strait to the southermost boundary of Chili, and the products of these regions taken back by the same way, and that this will become the favourite, as it will undoubtedly be the easiest and cheapest route to the Empires of China and Japan and to the whole Eastern Asia, as well to the gold regions of Australia.

From the Grenada Weekly Record April 4. The subjoined notice of a highly interesting occurrence in the Colony of British Guiana, is deserving of a more prominent place in our columns, than its insertion amongst our ordinary items of "Colonial Intelligence." It must swell the breast of every descendant of Africa, with emotions most pleasurable and gratifying : þÿ "Sunday the 4th of March was rendered remarkable by the ordination of the Revd. Mr. Mackenzie. This encouraging fact for the African race deserves more than ordinary attention, proving, if it had not been abundantly demonstrated already, the adaptation of special treaty with New Granada; and the African to the highest branches of human learning, or to the sacred calling of the minister of religion. Trained un-

ed Archdeacon Fothergill, Mr. Mackenzie early gave proofs of ability, which were not lost on his kind patron. He initiated him in the classics, and having watched over his progress for some time, sent him to Queen's College, where he continued to improve rapidly. The Right Reverend Patron, to his honor, saw at once the opportunity thus afforded of doing an act of graceful justice to this injured race, and assumed the charge of his education. Having gone through the course at Queen's College with credit to the institution Jnd to himself, he left it with the reputation of a good Latin and Greek scholar, and was transferred for his theological studies to the newly founded College of St. Augustine's, at Canterbury. On the completion of his three years' term of study, he reckoning upon any increase of traffic returned to his country, eager to make his talents and acquirements available among those who had known him in early youth, and his ordination on Sun-

day was a gratifying testimony to the earnest zeal with which he had answered the kind efforts of his friends and patrons, and the crowds that were attracted to hear his first discourse, attested their delight at his success. But it is not his mere human acquirements which form the chief elements of his usefulness; it is his deep, earnest desire to be of use among his countrymen, and to devote himself to religion. These are the great results of the experiment, which make its triumph so gratifying. May this be an inducement to many to enter on the same course." þÿ "Colonist," March 7.

Menschikoff, whose random wit, has a reputation in Russia, apologises characteristically enough for the comparative veracity of his latter despatches: þÿ 'I had a dream last night; I stood at the gates of Paradise; without the gates was Saint Peter dangling his keys. While 1 was waiting to take my turn there came up three hundred British soldiers who begged admittance, as they had died at the Alma, fighting for their country. St. Peter referred to Lord Raglan's despatches, and finding the soldier's tale to be true, let them in. Next came three hundred French soldiers, who also begged admittance, as they had died at Alma fighting for France and their Emperor. St. Peter turned over the file of the Moniteur and passed the Frenchmen through the gates. Next came up a thousand Russian soldiers, who begged admission into Paradise, for they had died in the Dobrudscha, fighting for the Czar, under Prince Gortschakoff against the infidel troops of Omar Pasha. But St. Peter shook his head as he held up the Invalide Rvsse, containing the despatches of Prince Gortschakoff, in which the loss of the Russians was described as insignificant. 1 Go,' said St. Peter, 'I have admitted the British soldiers, for I find their names in Lord Raglan's despatches. 1 have admitted the French, for I find their names in the Monileur ; but Prince Gortschakoff says nothing of your deaths. You are impostors and can have no place in Paradise.' And so I saw these poor Russian soldiers wander away outcast and forlorn, and it

seemed to me that they were doomed to wander for ever. When I awoke, I resolved to endeavor to conciliate my duty to the Emperor with my desire to gain admittance for our soldiers into Paradise. þÿ Leader.

On Friday, 20th instant, about an hour previous to the Levee, alluded to in our last number, the following Address was presented to our much beloved and esteemed former Governor, by a deputation consisting ol Messrs. Beech, Brown , Keulsch Abbott ,
3 tr <o m a a t aa FRO .II THE INHABITANTS OF THE ISLAND OF STA. CRUZ TO j His Excellency Governor H. D. F. FEDDERSEN Knigiit Commander of the Royal Order of Dannebrog.

Sir ! We the undersigned inhabitants of the island ofSta. Cruz cannot witness the departure ofYour Excellency without i publicly expressing t lie feelings of respect and attachment towards you which ani-

so soon leaving this government. The state of this island when Your Excellency first took over the office of Governor was far from satisfactory ; itsresources had been greatly impaired, the progress of social reorganisation and of needful reform been interrupted and public authority itself weakened. Your Excellency, however, entrusted by our mostgraciousSovereign with the Draftof a Colonial Law, calculated to establish a more explicit intercourse and close connexion between the mother country and this distant portion of the kingdom, has succeeded in calling into life an institution which, we trnst, will prove of lasting benefit to a community, the public opinion and general interests of which were up to that period scarcely represented with the Danish government and the Danish people. We venture to assert, that we have Your þÿExcellency s i strenuous exertions and kind mediation in a great measure to thank for the enact- ! ment of sundry useful anil important measures, partly proposed by the Council, partly emanating from yourself, and feel fully convinced that the postponement of other equally desirable public arrangements has been caused by circumstances over which you had no control. Thus Your Excellency has to the fullest extent of the powers delegated to you done your best to remedy grave defects and evils, and has thereby at once secured a lasting claim upon our grateful remembrance, whilst at the same

gress of your administration denoted a continual and uninterrupted solicitude for the welfare of the colony and measures, just as wise as energetic, shielded it as well from inward disturbances, when attempted, as from the imminent peril of a deadly epidemic which, had it not been for the unswerving consistency of the principles upheld by your gotor Smith, the Reverend þÿO Ryan, vernment, might have proved equally pernicious and appalling to Sta. Cruz as it has been to the sister island. But whilst we have thus briefly dwelt upon the merits of the official, we cannot forget the qualities of the private man, which will endear your memory to every body that values true loyalty, unvarying affability, real kindness and the beneficial example of a dignified life, which must he of double import and significance when set by a man in high | authority. However, Your Excellency is so fully aware of the sincere and deep interest which this community has felt and will ever feel in the prosperity of yourself and that promising and hopeful young family which have been bestowed upon you as a comfort, and according to the Fiat of the Almighty, also as a solace in after life, that we assuredly can part from you with the heartfelt prayer, that He may hold His gracious and protecting handover themandyou, to whatever new vocationyoumay be summoned, and ifwe may be allowed once more to revert to those public ties, which have hitherto , R. connected Your Excellency with the isl- Finlay and J. If. Bart junior: þÿ and of Sta. Cruz, we will beg; leave to ex-

press our firm conviction, that your good will and sympathy with us will not be affected by time and distance, but that the real interests of this community will in you henceforth possess an enlightened and zealous advocate in the councils of the mother country. YVe remain Your þÿExcellency s most obedient and devoted. Sta. Cruz 23rd April 1855

His Excellency replied as follows: Gentlemen ! It has. been highly gratifying to me to listen to the kind expressions that have just fallen from the lips of my honoured friend, with regard to my public acts and domestic position. It has been said that I have zealously endeavoured to contribute to the welfare of this Colony and I confess with joy, that that was precisely the feeling that strengthened mv mind in the fulfilment of my calling. It is the lot of but few to see their public efforts acknowledged and appreciated, but in enjoying this flattering exception it is my duty to acknowledge the strong support which I in all my undertakings have received from the kind feeling of the inhabitants and from those gentlemen who according to their position were called to be my counsellors. I have carried into execution the ideas and plans of the Minister, who represents the affairs of the Colony before the throne of our most gracious sovereign the King. The former Minister, Count Sponneck, is no longer in possession of the portfolio of the Ministry of Finances ; he has always evinced a great interest for the colonial affairs, and if in one instance the expectations of the inhabitants have not been fully realized þÿ i allude to the Law on Compensation þÿ this lias not been owing to any want of benevolent feeling, but to the exhausted condition of the Stale Treasury after a long and bloody war. þÿ i rejoice m observing, that his successor Colonel Andrae, with equal warmth suppoits the colonial interests and i am happy to in

form you, that the last packet brought to this Government the intelligence that the Budget anil five drafts of ordinances, respecting divers relations oi the Colony, have been sanctioned by His Majesty the King almost in the same sense and extent in which they were passed by the Colonial Council, and 1 beg to remark that only one of these Uraits has been , subjected to some alteration which the interest of the Crown required. Gentlemen, you haveappretlalcd those steadfast and uiidevialiiig principles that 1 have been carried through in the administration of the public affairs. 1 am about to give over my command into oilier hands, but I believe 1 may assure you that this will not cause any change in those principles. The harmony, so happily prevailing in the views entertained by my successor and myself must afford sufficient guarantee in this respect. Gentlemen, you will easily conceive,
3 If

that it is with feelings of a mingled nature that I soon retire from this Island. I have here spent happy days and gloomy hours, and both will leave a lasting remembrance in me: joys and sorrows unite in forming strong impressions, ceasing only with life itself. 'That noble and generous feeling which is so predominant a feature in the people ol this Island has always attracted me in a high j degreeand I am bound to this soil by many ties of friendship and attachment. It will therefore be an easy task for me to comply with the wish you have just now expressed : that 1, though far removed from these Islands, should work for their welfare, if fate grants me an occasion to do so. And thus I with great satisfaction embrace this opportunity to return you my heartfelt thanks for the praise you have bestowed upon me!

OIlITlJAItY. On the 3d instant Colonel Peter De Nelly, Knight of Dannebrog, departed this life, aged 78 years. The deceased had filled for many years the situation of Inspector of Customs at Christiansted, and also that of Stadshauptmand andChief of the Militia in this Island. In his public capacities he performed his duties to the entire satisfaction of his Government, as a private individual he was gentle, kind and humane. In his days of prosperity, he was generous and bountiful, and when fortune no longer smiled on him, he was yet ever ready to share his mite with those who in distress applied to him, and never was he known to dismiss a suffering fellow creature unrelieved. Such was the tenor of his whole life, and his memory will be cherished by many friends and fellow | subjects who have received benefits from his kind and charitable hand.

The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted , Friday the 4 th May 1855. The European Mails which were brought out to St. Thomas by the Steamer Tyne arrived here Wednesday afternoon by the Schooner þÿ Schol- able than it was the previous day, alþÿten. There is nothing of any great importance in the papers. The Russians were busily engaged with their preparations for the defence of St Petersburg ; the whole of the bridges on the Lower Neva, built of granite, have been demolished and thrown into the bed of the river, to render it impassable for large ships of war. Their fleet is fully armed, manned and victualled, and a light flotilla, consisting of 300 gun boats, is fitted out. A force of 120,000 men is concentrated in the Baltic provinces and round St. Petersburg. On the night of the 22d March the Kussians attacked the French lines at Sebastopol ; but were repulsed with great slaughter. The French fought with remarkable energy. The loss of both French and English amounts to about 200 men, and that of the Russians to 8 or 000 men. On the morning of the 24th a flag of truce was sent in by the allies with a proposition to the Kussians for an armistice to bury the dead, which were lying in numbers þÿ five or six Kussians to every Frenchman and Englishman þÿ in front of the Round Tower and Mamelon, and, after some delay, an answer in the affirmative was returned, and it was arranged that two hours should be granted for collecting and carrying away the dead on both sides. THE TURKISH CONTINGENT FOR THE CRIMEA CAMPAIGN. The Turkish contingent is to be recruited chiefly among the Albanians of Epirus and Macedonia. This may perhaps be the commencement of a new military system for Turkey. Tbe admission of Christians to tbe right and duty of bearing arms in the most disputed question relative to Turkey. It is a reform which would carry with it every other, and without itjio Tanzimat or firman will be of the least effect. In a Christian village, eight miles from Beicos, and almost within sight of the capital the unarmed inhabitants were lately expelled from their houses by the attack of armed Turks, and compelled to take refuge in the mountain. If this be the case close to Constantinople, it may easily be guessed what is the state o( things in Macedonia and the heart ot Asia Minor. The arming of the Albanians, both Mussulman and Christian, and their submission to military discipline, would prepare the way for an indiscriminate conscription throughout the empire, and be, perhaps, the best guarantee for the future good government of thecountry- The measure, however, must be gradually carried out. It is impossible to expec an immediatet levy of soldiers fit for active warfare against the Russians. The Albanian will not so readily throw of his wild and predatory habits, nor can he be formed into a soldier, except by officers who have gained a knowledge of the race to which he belongs and the language which he speaks.

The Indian officers are certainly the best qualified for the task ; they had better, however, not attempt to treat the Albanian as if he were a Sepoy, or they may endanger their own lives and the success of the whole enterprise. It is not the first time that England has had Albanians in her service. A body of them were under Lord W. Bentinck in Sicily during the last war, and are said to have been satisfactory troops. The employment of these foreign corps is therefore no new fact in English policy. When the British besieged Genoa towards the close of the war the army was composed of men of eleven different nations, all officered by Englishmen. If the experience gained in past years be applied to the present circumstances, there is every reason to believe that the result will he equally fortunate.

THE SIEGE OF SEBASTOPOL. March 27. þÿ Yesterday there was a heavy bombardment at Sebastopol, which was sustained on both sides with great energy; but gradually the fire of the Russians became weaker, and was at last entirely silenced, as the Russian guns that were brought into play were for the most part destroyed. There was no attack with the bayonet. Within the last few days it was observed from the heights of the allied camps that large caravans of inhabitants were leaving tlie town, inclusive of women and children, with goods and chattels. At the head of this expedition, which took the direction towards Bakchi Serai, there was a procession with holy flags, and the rear of the same was formed by thirty or forty Cossacks, whose duty was doubtless two fold, viz., to protect and at the same time to watch the expedition.

The main part of the ultimatum sent by M. Drouvn de Lliuys is generally said to be the destruction of the fortress of Sebastopol. He is instructed, it is stated, to insist that erection of forts at Sinope and Varna would be but a source of future trouble, instead of a solid counterbalance to Russian power in the Euxine, and, instead of proposing that the Black Sea shall be open to ships of war of all nations, he will offer to shut | it up entirely by treaty against the na- ! vies of the whole world, leaving it free ! as a commercial lake for merchantmen I only.

One of the Russian officers, who spoke French fluently, asked, during the late flag of truce, with a smile, how long We intended to stay in the Crimea. þÿ Till Sebastopol is þÿtaken, was the reply. þÿ In that case, you will have to wait all your þÿlifetime, was the rejoinder.

The following detailed account is vivid, and full of interest: Camp above Sebastopol, March 23. A sortie made by the Russians last night, first against the French advanced trench, and subsequently against the advanced works of the English, near the Mamelon redoubt, led to considerable loss on all sides, but chiefly on that of the attacking force. The slope of the Mamelon Hill is strewed with the Kussian dead, and many of their bodies are lying in the foss within our and the French line of breast works. The following appears to be the most connected account of the attack of the 22d and 23d ; and the details, as they become known by degrees, are found to accord with it. At about 11 p. m., or a little after, the French were busily employed in advancing their zig-zag, and connecting the ambuscades, which they had taken from the Russians in front of their advanced work at the foot of the Mamelon Hill. Three companies of the 3d Regiment of Zouaves, the regiment which lately suffered near the same spot, were defending the ambuscades, and some men of the 30th Regiment of the line were working under the direction of the Engineers. The evening had been clear, and the new moon and stars had given sufficient light to render visible objects within ordinary range, but the moon set early and the sky became clouded shortly after. Taking advantage of this darkness, a Russian force advanced against the French. They seemed to have formed behind the redoubt, and, dividing into two columns,

to have come round the hill, both on the right and on the left, throwing out their skirmishers as they advanced. In this way they contrived to pass the ambuscades on either flank, keeping onward towards the main line of entrenchment about fifty yards further on. It was not until just as the Russians had reached the parapet of the trench, that the soldiers in the ambuscades found themselves surrounded. Contrary to their usual custom, the Russians preserved the strictest silence, and it was only when they commenced the actual onslaught against the troops in the advanced work, and against those in the ambuscades, that they shouted their usual shrill hurrah. The men in the trench seem to have been taken completely by surprise, not having had any warning from their comrades who were working in the ambuscades. To effect their entrance on the French left of the trench, which still remains open near the edge of the rapine, the junction with the extreme right of the English advanced line of work not being yet accomplished, the Russians resorted to a stratagem employed once before by them with success. As they entered the trench the French soldiers started and were about to fire, when an officer advanced, and in nous sommes des amis þÿ a quiet undertone said, þÿ des Anglais and JVe iirez pasþÿ þÿ, the French officer then gave the order which prevented his men from at once firing and giving the alarm. The attack commenced on the right, the Russians

jumping upon the parapet, but in a moment it was universal. The troops in the ambuscades found themselves cut off from the trench, and completely surrounded. The troops in the trench itselt found themselves attacked by an overpowering force, and, keeping up a fire against their assailants, were at first compelled to retire. But the desperate struggle was at the ambuscades. The Zouaves fought like madmen, and numbers fell from the fire of their Minies, and from wounds inflicted by their bayonets and by blows from the butt-ends of their pieces, as they became closely pressed. It was only when they found all efforts unavailing against the powerful force arrayed against them on all sides, when'they found themselves destitute of all support from reinforcements from the works in their rear þÿ that the Zouaves fell back, which they did fighting as they retired. A serious proportion of their small band fell killed or wounded. On reaching the trench they had still to fight for possession of the ground, but shortly after supports arrived, and the Russians were driven from the work with great slaughter. At first the attack was confined to the French works on the Mamelon Hill. There were 800 men in Ihe corresponding advanced works on the English side, but as the entrenchments comprising the second and third parallels on Frenchþÿman Hill, s and the batteries connected with them, extend over very long lines of ground, this force was very widely scattered. They consisted of troops

from the 97th, 34th, 7th, 19th and 90th Regiments, and were under the immediate order of Lieut.-Col. Kelly, of the 34th Regiment. When the attack on the French commenced, the fire from the men in the ambuscades against the Russians on their left flank fell thickly amongst the English on the extreme right of the third parallel. This end of the work, like that on the left of the French, was open, and separated by little more than the breadth of the ravine. The troops were therefore ordered to move a little higher up the entrenchment, in a direction toward the left. Some time elapsed after the fighting had become general in the French works, when some troops were observed moving along the English trench. As they had not come over the parapets from the other side, but had moved in a direction from the French work, it was at first taken for granted that these were French soldiers. The mistake was discovered, and our men were ordered to charge. At first stooping and moving quietly, they came upon the enemy almost unobserved; but when within a short distance they poured in a volley, gave an English hurrah, and charged. The Russians did not wait to see what a small number was coming down upon them, but clambering over the parapet and running along the trench towards the ravine, they fled in confusion. Captain the Hon. Cavendish Browne, of the 7th Fusiliers, and Captain Hedley Vicars, of the 97th Regiment, appear to have particularly distinguished themselves by their gallantry. Capt. Vicars,

leading on some men of his regiment, chased the enemy over the parapet, and followed toward the ravine. His arm was elevated in the act of waving his sword, while lie was turning to cheer on the men, when a hall struck him in the arm-pit, and he fell. He died on his way to camp, while being carried on a stretcher, either from haemorrhage or from the ball having penetrated the chest. Captain Browne was also killed, and his body was found to he penetrated by. no less than tour halls in the chest and two in other parts of the body. About the same time that some of the Russians entered the third parallel at the open end near the ravine another body contrived to get into the work by mounting over the parapet at some distance off on the left, at a spot from which the covering party had been drawn off for the purpose of defending the right. They also were quickly driven back. I have not heard our exact loss in accomplishing these objects, but about thirtyfour wounded onlv have been brought into camp. Lieutenant-Colonel Kelly, who commanded the covering party on þÿFrenchman s Hill, is missing, and fears are entertained for his safety. Lieutenant William Jordan, of the 34th Regiment, who had exchanged duty with another officer for the evening, was killed. Major Gordon, of the Royal Engineers, who for some time had command of the siege operations, and whose name is so completely associated with the works on þÿFrenchman s Hill, and many of those now held by our allies on the

right, was wounded severely, having been struck by two musket balls in the arm. The French loss is very much greater; as many as 130 killed, and nearly 400 wounded being named. As appears generally to happen, the chief loss was among the Zouaves. Some of the Imperial Guard, who were brought as a reinforcement, also suffered severely. Immense bodies of French troops moved towards the Mamelon after the attack, in the expectation that it would he removed, but the troops remained within their respective lines for the remainder of the night. Lord Raglan was at the scene of contest at an early hour this morning. Among the dead left in the advanced work on þÿFrenchman sHill is an officer, who was supposed to he a Russian, but papers on his person lead to the supposition that he was a Greek in Russian pay. Three other bodies are recognised as being those of Armenians. The French also stale that there were many Greeks fighting against them in their attack. March þÿ24, -All last night the French and Russians fired heavily, and some skirmishing went on at the rifle pits, but without any particular result. The French do not appear to gain ground upon the rifles beyond the three pits which they captured some time since. Yesterday evening a flag of truce was sent in by the enemy to ask permission to remove and bury their dead, and today, between the hours of twelve and

£ 'JR I) S SSL A V it 8 two, has been appointed for that purpose. The dead still remain all round the breastwork exactly as they fell. Upon the body of one of their non-commissioned officers 36 gold pieces were found by one of our men, and several of the men killed are in the ordinary dress of Levantine Greeks, as if taken from the inhabitants of the towns. Lord Raglan has forbidden firing on the towns from motives of policy, as it is said. The French Emperor is, according to general rumour, expected here on the 27th. The electric telegraph between Lord þÿRaglan s head quarters and the trenches has been completed. It is blowing a heavy gale, but the weather continues fine and dry. No prospect of the fire being opened for another ten days or a fortnight to come. Ten long guns have yet to be mounted in different batteries.

INCIDENTS CONNECTED WITH THE WAR. According to a letter from the Crimea in the Malta Times , the Russians did not come to the determination to sink the vessels which they had lately sent lo the bottom in the harbour of Sebastopol until they had removed them from place to place, and ascertained that it was quite impossible to station them in any place where they would not be exposed to the fire of the enemy. A St. Petersburg correspondent, writing on the 3 1 si ult., says, þÿ To-day an ordinance has been published concerning the beaut of the soldiers. The Emperor has deigned to order, first, that the soldiers who mount guard on week days shall not be required to dye either their hair or whiskers; and secondly. on Sundays and feast-days they must mount guard with their hair and whiskers waxed and þÿdressed. It is also staled, that the Emperor Alexander intends to visit Helsingfors, with his brother Nicholas, before the commencement of operations in the Baltic.

THE WAR IN ASIA COMMENCED. The first of the spring operations on the coast of Circassia has just been attempted þÿ attempted, rather than executed On the 14th, the English steamers Leopard, High-' fiver, and Viper, which had been engaged for a fortnight previously cruising along the eastern seaboard of the Euxinc, made an attack upon the Russian fort at Soudjakkale, garrisoned by a force of some 5 000 men. It had previously been arranged with some of the native chiefs that, simultaneously wiih the bombardment by the English ships of war, an attack should be made on The land side by a numerous body of Circassians. Accordingly, on the morning of the 14th, the steamers opened fire upon the fort, which speedily replied with some very heavy metal. This lasted till noon, when, finding that from some unaccountable and unknown reason the Circassians had not made a single aggressive movement, the commanders of the ships, seeing the futility of a merely sea attack, ceased firing and weighed anchor, having sustained a total loss of four killed and twelve wounded. The Leopard carried off twenty balls in her hull, and the Highflyer seven-

teen Though, through the strange drawback on the part of the Circassians, this attempt was thus resultless, there are signs of further and early operations along this coast Persia is assembling 50,000 men on the Turkish frontier, and her attitude is still suspicious. It is said that Russia is feeding her with hopes of the cession of some of the Turkish provinces. Mr. Murray, the English Minister, is ably opposing this influence.
Colonel Kelly, of the 34th, is a prisoner at Sebastopol, slightly wounded. Captain Montague, of the Royal Engineers, is also a prisoner, and is not wounded.

The importance of one vote is illustrated in every closely-contested election, but the value of one letter every man is made to feel who writes for the press. From the discovery of the art of printing down to this present, when there is so much of it that one sometimes wishes the good old times were back again when there were no books, the blunders of the types have been the most provoking experiences to the author, and perplexing or amusing to the reader. No book in the world has been so often printed, none has suffered so much in printing, as the Bible. þÿ The vinegar þÿBible is so called from the misprint of the title to the twentieth chapter of Luke ; þÿ the Parable of the Vineþÿyard printed the Parable of the Vine- was þÿ gar þÿ It was printed in 1717, in England. The þÿStationer Company, s having a monopoly of the Bible printintr business, were mulcted in a ruinous fine for issuing an edition in which the not was left out of the seventh commandment ! But even worse Ran that, was the fate of a poor woman. She was the wife of a printer, and had knowledge of the business enouyh, and mischief too, to enter his office after the types were all ready to print an e iition of the Bible, and taking out the word Lord from Genesis iii. 16, and putting in its place the word fool, she destroyed the sentence of subjection to her husband pronounced upon Eve, so that instead of reading þÿ he shall be thy þÿlord, the passage appeared þÿ he shall be thy fool þÿ The poor woman actually paid for her folly by the forfeit of

her life. But some copies of that edition have been bought by collectors at a very high price. One of our own Bible societies committed the most amusing of all Scriptural blunders in printing an edition in which the 27th verse of Galatians fourth is murdered. The Apostle says, þÿ For the desolate hath many more children than she which hath an husband which the printers made to read, þÿ than she which hath an hundred." Some copies of that edition are abroad, but great pains were taken to get them all in. We sympathize with the author who received the last sheet of his elegantly printed book, and was shocked to find that where he had written Pope Gregory, the types had made him say Tom Gregory 1 But it was not too late. He was just in time to correct it, and carefully putting the Pope in the margin, that the printers might be sure to get it right, he thought no more of it till the bound volume was in hand, with the error rectified from Tom Gregory into Pope Tom Gregory.

The Military Gazette of Turin states that the expeditionary corps is to remain pro tempore at Constantinople, with the French Imperial Guard. This is to be the army of reserve of the allies. The Gazette considers the destination assigned to the Piedmontese contingent as a proof of deference and esteem on the part of Napoleon III. for the Sardinian army.

The Russians have lately adopted an imitation of the ball used in the Minie rifle. Many cartridges were found in the pouches of men killed on the night of the 22d inst. with the conical ball and iron cup at the base. The cup is very roughly made. There were also found cartridges containing two halls, connected with each other by a spiral of brass wire. The spiral, when closed, occupiedaspaceof about two-thirdsof an inch in length ; when drawn out, was capable of being stretched to a length approaching to half a foot. This is a new device ; it is the application of the chain-shot to small firearms. þÿ Observer April 15.

From the Observer, April 15, 1855. PROGRESS OF THE ADVANCED SQUADRON OF THE BALTIC FLEET.

On Saturday morning, the 31st ult., the advanced squadron of the Baltic fleet had entered the (Jauegai, and sighted the Island of Anholt : a separation was then ordered, the senior officer, Captain Watson, taking the route through the Great Bell to Kiel with the Euryalus and Conflict, and the remainder, under Captain Yelverton, proceeding on direct through the Sound to Elsinore; the Imperieuse, Euryalus, and Conflict, to Kiel, the Arrogan, Amphion, Tartar, Cossack, Esk, Desperate, and Archer to Elsinore. At the same time the Desperate was detached to Wingo Sound to ascertain the state of that anchorage, and send on the colliers (if any there) to Elsinore. On Sunday morning the ships under Captain Yelverton anchored off Elsinore, having encountered much opposition from the flows of loose ice in passing up the Sound. I'he harbour of Elsinore was completely blocked up, and no opening could be seen in the direction of Copenhagen. The | ice continuing to move down in increasing quantities, the steam was ordered to be kept up; the pressure on the ships soon became too heavy for either anchors or cables, and of the four ships three þÿ namely, the Arrogant> Esk, and Tartar þÿ parted from their anchors ; the Arrogant's was lost in the attempt to weigh it, but the others were fairly dragged away, and carried down some miles in the ice-field before they could clear themselves fho ships then anchored a few miles to the northward, behind Kullen-point ; but during the night considerable quantities of ice con-

tinued to pass them, without, however, occasioning further damage, and this morning (April2) soon after daylight they again weighed, and proceeded under steam, with as much speed as the circumstances would permit, through the Sound to Landscrona, a small but secure harbour on the coast of Sweden, about twelve miles distant from, and within sight of Elsinore. Here they arrived on the afternoon of the 2d instant, and with the assistance of the harbour-master and pilots all were (notwithstanding that the ice in the harbour was still unbroken) got inside and safely moored head and stern ; the harbour itself, inclosed between an island and the mainland, is very small, but in no part less

of the largest size can lay in safety, let the wind blow from whatever quarter it may ; but the approach is intricate, and the difficulty of getting in much increased when obstructed by ice. The Desperate rejoined the squadron from Wingo Sound on the morning of the 2d, having been unable to get inside on account of the ice. Two or three vessels, supposed to be colliers, had contrived to get in, but with considerable damage, and one had been totally lost. The Desperate has been again sent away with despatches for the senior officer. The Sound is at present pretty free from ice, as far as can be seen from this (Landscrona). but the pilots and the people here say,

that for the next ten days it will be constantly passing in immense flows, which no amount of steam power would enable us to resist. The Belts are also, they say, full of ice, and Kiel harbour completely blocked up. In fact, great surprise is expressed at our having come out so soon, as for some weeks nothing can be done in the Baltic, and our remaining here must be attended with more or less risk.

The five ships of the flying squadron which arrived at Elsinore on Sunday were obliged to put to sea again on account of the icefields which threatened to surround them. Some of them lost their anchors and cables, and one got agrouud on the shoals called Sktberoe, where she remained for a couple of hours, but got off without damage. They have gone over to the Swedish side of the Sound, and will seek shelter, if practicable, in the harbour of Landscrona. Accounts from Stockholm state that the weather had at length changed, and a dead thaw set in, by which the snow was disappearing and the ice getting very rotten. The thermometer stood at 8 deg. Reaumur (50 deg. Farenheit).

® <Q a: X ii T 2 3» The Sun- Flower þÿ The great variety of valuable properties belonging to the sunflower seed has been more neglected than any other, when it ought to be paid more attention to. No plant produces such fine honey and wax, now becoming more valuable, arising out of the Russian and Turkish war, from whence very large quantities in times of peace are imported. When this seed is crushed as linseed is, it will produce the very finest oils in larger quantities in proportion to any other seed, for the table as well as the painter, particularly in mixing green and blue paints. Sir Allen Orockden, of Seal Grove, by Sevenoaks, has for many j years cultivated the sun-flower, for the purpose of feeding his sheep, pigs, poultry, rabbits, and pigeons. It makes most beautiful soap, particularly softening to the hnnds and

cake is superior to linseed for fattening cattle. Sheep, pigs, pigeons, rabbits, poultry of nil sorts, &c., will fatten rapidly upon it, and j prefer the seed to any other ; pheasants in particular, causing them to have a much more glossy plumage and to be plumper in body. This seed, when shelled, makes when ground the very finest flower for bread, particularly tea-cakes. No doubt the ladies will patronise it largely þÿ it is so sweet. It will grow in any corner that may be vacant, and make all forms have a most agreeable garden-like appearance. It should be planted about six niches apart, and about one inch deep, and when about one foot high should be earthed up; it then will require no further attention. Every single seed will produce one thousand or more ; the main head generally produces 800 to 1000 seeds, and there arc generallv four collaterals, producing 50 or 60 seeds each. But it is not the seed only that is so valuable þÿ the stalk is most so ; for, by treating il exactly as flax is, it will produce a fibre ns fine ns silk, and that in large quantiiics. And now that rags have become so valuable, nrising from the very unprecedented demand for paper, the stalk might be made useful for that purpose. On some grounds two crops j may be growing at the same time for when þÿ the planter has given his early potatoes their last hoeing, plant this seed twelve inches apart in the ridges. Some three or four years ago, one or two farmers cleared nearly £40 by their honey hivas only. What would this

be now that each of these bears so much Vega, and observing this plant growing so | higher price arising out of the Russian war ? Then why, gentlemen farmers, wijl you not march a little out of your old beaten track, and plant the sun-flower seed, that lias all important.-and profitable propel ties? The Chinese have it by thousands of tons, and worship it. There enn bo no doubt that many of their silk goods have a large portion of the sun-flower in them.

Wore Work for Harry, Several shipping houses in this city have for some time been engaged in procuring guano from Isle Aves, a small island situated in lat. 15, Ion. 60 1-2, about 400 miles from the coast of Venezuela, 200 miles south of St. Thomas, and 150 miles west of GuadaJoupe This island contains a large quantity of guano, and several cargoes of it have been recently brought to this port. A few weeks since, while the crews of our vessels were en-

gaged in securing their cargoes, they were driven away by an armed ship belonging to the government of Venezuela, and the island taken possession of by a body of soldiers. Now, the question is, to whom does this island belong? There is an island called Aves, just off the coast of Venezuela, which undoubtedly belongs to that government ; hut the Isle Aves we refer to was formerly under the Danish flag, and has been claimed by the French. At all events, it is pretty certain that Venezuela lias no just claim to it. Here is a chance for Mr. Marcy : and as there probably is more guano on this little island than on the whole group of Gallipagos, it is certainly worth his attention. It would be well enough to settle the owner-ship, so that our shipmasters may know who to deal with.
New Broth for the Sick.

Professor Liebig, the distinguished chemist, has recently put forth the following recipe for a new broth for the sick. The peculiarity is, that it is prepared without heat: For one portion of broth take half a pound of freshly-killed meat, (beef or chicken,) cut it in small pieces, add to it 1 1-6 lb. of distilled water, to which liasbeen added 4 drops ofof pure chlorydi ic (muriatic) acid, and half to one drachm of common salt, mix them well together. After standing an hour, the whole is strained through a conical hair sieve, such as is ordinarily used in the kitchen, allowing it to pass through without pressing or squeezing. The portion passing through first being cloudy, it is again poured through the sieve, and this process repeated until it becomes perfectly clear. Upon the residue of the meat remaining in the sieve, half a pound of distilled water is poured in small portions. In this manner about one pound of liquid (cold extract of meat) is obtained of a red color j and pleasant meat broth taste. It is administered to the sick, cold, by the cup full, according to their inclination. It must not he heated, as it becomes cloudy thereby, and n thick coagulum of meat, albumen and hematin is deposited. þÿ Naussan Guardian.

Having copied into our last number an extract from the St Thomas " Tidende" relative to an | accident to the R. M. S. Toy, we feel it our < duty to publish also the following letter addressed to the Editor ol that paper by the Superintendent at St. Thomas : þÿ To the Editor of the " St. Thvma Tidende."

St. Thomas, July 7, 1855.. Sir, þÿ I hope you will be good enough to correct a serious nm-statemcut made in your last paper þÿ namely, that tlie Royal Mail Steam Packet Tay had grounded at St. John's, Porto Rico, in consequence of which she bad damaged her machinery, aud had to discharge coals to get off. The facts were simply as follows : þÿ the ship was about starting from the Buoy at St. John's, aud on the Captain giving the order to go ahead, when she was pointed down the fairway, the machinery refused duty, something having become deranged, when the Captain gave orders to drop the anchor, hut before the ship could bo brought up, she geutly drifted into shallower water, and touched the mud, where she remained some hours till the tide rose, when she was warped off' by her own hawsers to the Buoy. In justice to a young Commander, who shewed great tact and judgment under the circumstances, bringing his ship up to St. Thomas with ouly one engine to be repaired while the coaling went on, to save time, I hope you will allow this note to appear in your impression of to-day the Com- þÿ mander in question (Captain Moir), having expressed much annoyauce on reading was per, as the statement therein made your last pa- of a nature to seriously injure his professional reputation. I may add, as regards the Toy, that she started for Southampton yesterday at 10 a. m., with her engines in good working order. Your obedient servant, J. B. CAMERON, Supt. M. S. r. Co.

To (lie Public ! Already have we been accused of being guilty of harsh treatment in refusing to insert in the " Avts" advertisements in cases where the c ash did not accompany the same. We are yet to learn why an establishment may not have the

right to determine its own business-conditions ; and once having done so, to adhere to them. We have before stated in our columns, and now repeat, that all advertisements must be accompanied with the cash, as otherwise no notice whatever will be taken of them. We mean to offend no one ; our only motive is to do a cash business ; and we are, therefore, quite at a loss to conceive how in justice any gentleman can fancy himself aggrieved because we will not subject ourselves to the charge of uttering what we do not intend to fulfil. We have lost a subscriber by this means. For this we are sorry ; but we will rather lose them all than be faithless to our own principles. We will abide by the decision of the public, whether we have given cause of offence in the discharge of the duty we owe ourselves. In refusing insertion to advertisements in cases stated above, we do not mean to doubt the ability, or even the willingness, of the party to pay when dunned, but we cannot spare our workmen from their business to be running for always forgotten, or which " cannot be paid days for au amount which, from its siuallness, is to-day" for " want of change."

Berlin, June 12. The official reports of the state of Sebastopol received in St. Petersburg at the beginning of this month no longer exhibit the same satisfactory picture of things as previous to the last bombardment. The south side of the town has suffered very considerably ; a number of houses are piles of ruins, of others only the external walls are distinguishable ; the theatre, which is endeared to the Russians by so many recollections, has ceased to exist. The northern portion of the town has by no means suffered so much, but yet there is hardly a house there the walls or roof of which have not been perforated by grenade, shell, ball, or rocket, or the window panes and frames of which have not been destroyed by fragments of exploding shells. The inhabitants of Sebastopol have, however, by no means deserted the town ; with few exceptions, they continue to occupy their houses, even though battered. In the shops and warehouses traffic is represented as being kept up with but little diminution ; even the hotels were not shut. The only promenade which is left the fashionable world in those parts is the new Boulevard in the neighbourhood of Kasarski's monument, from which there is a fine view, on the one side, of the surrounding mountains, with the allied camp, its trenches, and its fortifications ; on the other side, over the sea, with the allied fleets keeping ward and watch over the Crimea. On the northern side steamers and boats are seen all day and all night plying
to and from the Catherine Harbour, laden with gabions, fascines, balls, shells, powder, and materiel de guerre of all sorts ; while on the landing places stores of cannon and carriages, mortars,

The Emperor has allotted 200,000 silver roubles for the current and 100,000 for the following year, to be applied to the benefit of the sailors engaged in the defence of Sebastopol ; the moneys are to be derived from the surplus of the St. Petersburg and Moscow funds. Italy. Turin, June 11. As England is about forming a Foreign Legion it is very probable that it might be found desirable to raise riders as well as horses from the same districts, and, except Hungary and Transylvania, there is no part of Europe more capable perhaps of furnishing a body of cavalry suited particularly to serve as the eyes of the army than Central Italy. The men are active and intelligent, and, it may be safely asserted, for outpost duty would bo found infinitely more wide-awake than any of the Saxon race. A great deal has been said latterly about the irregular cavalry of India and its efficiency, but one great cause of its goodness is that the horse is the property of the rider or of his immediate commander and patron. On this principle, of course, it would be impossible to raise a corps in Europe for foreign service, but in every other respect there is no reason why a cavalry corps should not
be formed in Italy, which for quickness, intelligence and economy, should rival the celebrated Jacob's Horse of Bombay.

TRIMJDAD We would direct the attention of our scientific readers to the following extract from the Port of Spain Gazette: þÿ To the liditor of the 1'urt of Spain Gazette. Sir, þÿ I send yon an extract from a scientific journal relative to a mode of burning wet fuel, which would probably be applicable to mogass fresh from the mill. As it appears to me, that such an invention, if really a practical one, would be of enormous, I may almost say incalculable, importance to this island, more especially in seasons of uncertain weather, tike that of the present year; I have written to the British Consul at New Orleans, requesting him to furnish the Trinidad Corresponding Committee of the Society of Arts, of which 1 am Secretary, with all the information he can collect on the subject in Louisiana, where it is in progress of trial on mogass. I am, yours obediently, HAMILTON WARNLR. May Pith 1855.

"Mr. Moses Thompson, of Ringhampton, N. Y., has lately patented, and is now, with considerable success, introducing a furnace for the burning of very wet fuel, which appears likely to affect the mode of conducting some of our less important steam generating processes, and promises ultimately to succeed in sugar boiling, than which, perhaps, few discoveries are more desirable, Mr. Thompson has succeeded in burning wet tan, direct from the vats of some of our largest tanneries, and in generating therefrom an intensely white heat, sullicient to melt cast or wrought iron in a very few minutes. In tact , the high temperature generated and maintained in the furnaces, and the means adopted to attain this result form the main distinguishing features of the invention. One great error in previous attempts to burn wet fuel, has consisted in admitting more rather than less air to the wet fuel. Mr. Thompson constructs his grates somewhat in the ordinary manner, but with greatly diminished spaces between the bars, depending for a large portion of the oxygen on that set free by the decomposition of the water. The process completely consumes the fuel without the production of smoke, but this is accomplished only by having two or more furnaces in connection, and supplying fresh fuel to one only at a time. The necessary high temperature is maintained by having a furnace at some little distance from the boiler and thicklv casing them with fire brick and other non-conducting materials, allowing tl

flame and intensely heated gases to flow from the two furnaces into contact with the boiler after mixing together. The furnaces are ovens of brick, somewhat analogous in form, but more in temperature, to air or puddling furnaces for melting metals. The fuel is supplied through a cavity in the top of eacli furnace, and is allowed to pile itself up in a cone with no regard to equal distribution over the furnace of the grate. The flame passes off nearly horizontally into a mixing chanber, and thence to the boilers, under and through which is allowed to flow in a manner similar to that usually employed in utilizing the waste heat from the iron manufacture. One furnace only being supplied with fresh fuel at a time, the steam escaping is sure to find in the mixing chamber, which is merely a place of junction of the flue passages, a sufficiently high temperature to decompose it. The grand

%VA A T a 3, features of the invention consist, firstly, in carefully cherishing the heat ol the furnace to induce the production of an intensod high temperature ; secondly, in mixing the gases from fresh fuel with those from fuel previously well heated ; and thirdly, in admitting a very limited supply of air. The degree of temperature attained is not, of course, ascertainable, even approximately, without careful and expensive experiment ; but the fact that all metals introduced into the flue passages disappear very rapidly, and that the fire brick roof of the furnaces have an inconvenient habit of fusing and running down in vitreous streams, if proper precautions are not adopted, argues the existence of as high a temperature as any ordinarily employed in the arts. " The fuel principally employed in the furnaces thus far is net tan, oak tan, being more suitable than hemlock tan, because of its greater coherence when partially consumed. The process of combustion renders the mass highly porous, like honey comb, the lire percolating it from beneath in countless streams, which, in case of oak tan, increases in size until the whole is consumed, whilst with hemlock the mass is continually crumbling down and stopping the passages. Several experiments have been lately made on the sugar plantations of Louisiana, in burning the mogass, or crushed cane, direct from the rolls of the sugar mill. The only difficulty at present apprehended by the inventor relates entirely to the mode of

feeding the bulky and trashy material. Several eminent sugar planters in the vicinity of New Orleans, express their high hopes of its greatly increasing the efficiency of this species of fuel," þÿ Practical Mechanics Journal, March 1855, Page 271.

HANDWRITING. Hood gives some good advice upon this subject, which he submits to the particular attention of " poets and prosers, who aspire to write in miscellanies ; and, above all, the palpitating untried, who meditate the offer of their maiden essays to established periodicals." He advises these writers, to " take care to cultivate a good, plain, bold, round text ; to set lip Tomkins as well as I'ope or Dryden for a model, and to have an eye to their pot-hooks. " Of all things, therefore, he legible ; I and to that end, practise in penmanship. If you have ne\er learned, take six lessons of Mr. Carstairs. Re sure to buy the best paper, the best ink, the best pens, and then sit down and do the best you can, as the school-boys do þÿ put out your tongue, and take pains. So ye shall haply escape the rash rejection of a jaded editor ; so, having got in your hand, it is possible that your head may follow ; and so, last not least, ve may fortunately avert those awful mistakes of the press, which sometimes ruin a poet's snblimest effusion, by pantomimically transforming his 'roses' into 'noses;' his 'angels' into 'angles;' " and all his 'happiness' into pappiness.'

The Army Military Drf.ss A further alteration has taken place in the dress of the Royal Foot Artillery. The new cap is to be small in size, but similar in point of shape to that worn by the Horse Artillery. The covering of black fur is to display the novelty of having the white feather, royal arms, &.c., on the side instead of in the front. There
is to be no band. A scarlet bag is to flow from the top. The new design possesses for the soldier one desideratum, viz., that of lightness.

Mormons on Slavery. llrigham Young, the high priest of the Mormons at the Great Salt Lake, has recently issued a manifesto, in which he replies to charges brought against the Mormons by the people of the United States. lie states that the charge against the Mormons of being hostile to American slavery is a calumny. His words are: "The seed of Ham, which is the seed of Cain, descending through Ham, will, according to the curse put upon him, serve bis brethren, and be a ' servant of servants' to his fellow-creatures, until God removes the curse, and no power can hinder it. Rut the conduct of the whites towards the slaves will, in many cases, send both slave and master to hell. The black should be used like servants, and not like brutes; but they must serve. It is their privilege to live so as to enjoy many of the blessings which attend obedience to the first principles of the gospel, though they arc not entitled to the priesthood."

The European Mail of the 2nd July, per R M. Steam-ship La Plata, was landed at St. Thomas on Sunday night the 15th, and our correspondence by her reached here her the Vigilant. La Plata, with last evening by usual punctuality, had 13 days out, and brings the unexpected and painful intelligence of the death of Field- Marshal Lord Ragi.an, late Commander-in- Chief of the Forces in the Crimea. His Lordship expired on the 28th June. His death is said to have thrown a gloom over the whole Army. We publish to-day as much of the European news as we. can make room for, þÿ þÿ our extracts þÿ being principally from the þÿTimes and Obþÿserver. War Department, June 30, 1855. Lord Panmure has received intelligence from General Simpson, announcing the fatal termination of Lord þÿRaglan illness. s Until 4 p m. on the 28th II is Lordship had been progressing to the satisfaction of his medical attendants, when alarming symptoms developed themselves, attended with difficulty of breathing, which gradually increased. From 5 p. m. he was unconscious, aud from this period he gradually sank, until twenty-five minutes before 9, at which hour he died. The event has plunged the whole army into the most profound grief.

We have the great pain of announcing to our readers the first check received by the arms of the allies in the Crimea, and that check was a severe one Relying upon the late brilliant suc- 5 withdrawals amounting: to $ 126 71. j cess, and the advanced positions maintained in such close proximity þÿ the spirit and confidence of their troops and taking into account þÿ too prepared their guns and mortars for a ! simultaneous bombardment of the defences of Sebastopol þÿitself Lord Raglan and General Pelissier decided upon assaulting the MalakhofF Tower and the Redan Batteries, on the morning of the 18th, having commenced the heavy bombardment on the previous day. These attacks were made not merely with gallantry, but with a courage amounting to desperation. The French took actual possession of the Malakhoff Tower, and the British were twice within the Redan, and in the very inner works of Sebastopol ; but they could not maintain themselves there, when the Malakhoff, which commands it on the flauk, was once more in the hands of the Russians The guns of the ships were brought to bear on I the Malakhoff, which it was found impossible to retain, after it had been carried in the most gallant manner Roth the French and the English were therefore obliged to retreat to their established positions in front of the place; which, however, they effected in good order, and they have still not lost an inch of ground, although their further progress is arrested for the moment. - London Observer, Juno 24.

The despatches from General Pelissier, of the 19th and 20th June, which were published in the Moniteur of yesterday morning, suffice to provo that the check sustained by the allied forces in the assault of the 18th had neither abated their confidence nor materially raised the hopes of the enemy. In the night immediately following the unsuccessful attack a panic appeared to have seized the Russians, who flew to their guns and opened general a fire on the whole line of their works, although no one was threatening them. On the 20th the approaches of the besiegers on the side of the Central Ravine were driven so close that the enemy set fire to the little suburb at the bottom of the southern harbour, and in the meantime the allies were placing heavy guns on the Selinghinsk and Valhynan Battery, taken on the 7th of June, so as to command the great harbour. The tone of this brief but significant communication clearly shews that the failure of the assault on the Malahkoff Tower and the Redan has in no degree lessened the vigour with which the siege is being carried on, and the destruction by the Russians themselves of the suburbs of Sebastopol within their lines is a very strong proof of the increasing difficulty of the defence. The actual number of our own killed and wounded in the recent attack on the Redan is not. of that terrible amount which was at first supposed. When it was stated that the loss of our noble army was not less than 4,000, that was interpreted to mean the British loss alone and it

was inferred that, if we had lost so many the loss of the French must have been 10,000 or more. It now appears that the total loss of killed and wounded þÿ in the whole allied army does not exceed 4,000, of which our portion was just under 1,309. The number of non-commissioned officers and men killed is 144 and wouuded 1,058; the total number of officers killed and wouuded is 93 þÿ making the amount total 1,295. The enemy, it appears, boast that they have taken 600 French prisoners, which in the present state of our knowledge we can only suspect to be a Russian exaggeration.

The very serious news of losses in the highest places received by the late telegraphic messages, have thrown a gloom over the intelligence from the Crimea, which is not justified by other facts. The death of Captain Lyons in the very midst of his glorious successes, and the melancholy termination of Lord þÿRaglan searthly career, hav» thrown a gloom over the public mind, which com-

municates its dark shadow over other passing events Captain Lyons, of the Miranda, was a worthy son of a most worthy father. He sought every danger, where he could be useful to his country, and perished from a wound received in a close

reconnaissance of the strength of the þÿenemy s stronghold. Lord þÿRaglan s loss is all but irreparable. Beyond these deplorable losses there arc no reverses to be announced. The public mind runs fast in the train of misfortune.
