From the New York Courier and Enquirer OUR MINISTER TO ENGLAND We have frequently had occasion to allude to the admirable manner in which our country has been represented at the Court of St. þÿJames by j Mr. Buchanan, and of the kind relations existing between him and the English Cabinet, notwithstanding the idle rumours from Washington. Wo are happy to know that Mr. Buchanan is as popular with the people of London as he is with the Court ; and at the late Anniversary Dinner of þÿ the Royal Literary Fund þÿSociety, the Bishop of Oxford, who presided, made a most complimentary speech in regard to our Country, our People, our Literature, and our Minister, concluding with the following toast : þÿ The Literature and Science of the United States, and the American Minister Mr. Buchanan.121' Wc annex Mr. þÿBuchanan very s felicitous icply from the þÿ London þÿGlobe of the 25th May : þÿ Lord My , My Lords and Gentlemen : þÿ I esteem it a privilege to be invited to respond to this sentiment in favor of the literature and science of my country. The applause with which it has been greeted by the present distinguished company proves that it is no unmeaning compliment, but has proceeded from the heart. I am proud of the advance which my countrymen have made in literature and science, and am equally proud that this has been justly n. predated by a British audience of such high authority on questions of literature and science, that there can be no appeal from its decision to any higher tribunal. þÿ The time was when the question might have

been justly asked in this þÿcountry, who reads an American book ? That time has passed away ; and, judging by my own intercourse with English society, it might with equal justice be asked, j who has not read an American book ? I find that every where throughout the United Kingdom, the works of American authors are now ublished and circulated. These, however, bear ut a comparatively small proportion to the number and the variety of the works of distinguished

British authors, living and dead, published and circulated throughout the United States. In little more than half a century from the present hour, with the blessing of God, these works will be read and admired, will influence the life and conduct and the destiny of a hundred millions of intelligent Americans between the Atlantic with Pacific oceans, speaking the same language and yourselves. What a bond of union must this prove to be between the kindred nations ! þÿ It must not be inferred, that although proud of your approbation, we estimate our attainments in literature and science beyond their proper value. We freely admit that ours is nothing more than the early promise of a healthy and vigorous youth ; but we live in the confident hope that our maturity will more than justify this promise. þÿ We have but fairly commenced the task, but as we aim at excellence in literature and science, we shall never relax our efforts until, if possible, we may attain a | Jacc in the temple of fame on the same proud eminence with your- selves. þÿ We will þÿtry, yes, þÿ we will try þÿ This has become a motto of our country. þÿ We have many reasons for believing that we shall prove successful. Among the principal of these is the undoubted fact that the literature and science occupy that exalted position in the opinion of our countrymen to which they are so justly entitled. This is well calculated to give an impulse to ambitioD. There is no class amongst us who stand higher þÿ no, not one þÿ than

the class of eminent authors. For the truth of this assertion, I think I might with confidence sent. Such men are everywhere received appeal to the experience of gentlemen now in pre- th« United States as public benefactors. þÿ The republic of letters is a universal republic, and embraces within its limits all civilized nations. Several of its most distinguished representatives are now within the sound of my voice, and the educated people of all nations are their constituents and judges. These true representatives of the progress of civilization may fail to receive justice from their contemporaries, þÿ they may be too far in advance of their own age to be appreciated ; but posterity never fails to do them justice. Whilst the generations of politicians, and with rare exceptions, even of statesmen, pass away with the events with which they have been identified, and are forgotten , such names as those of Shakspcare, and Milton, and Locke, and Newton, flourish in immortal youth, and their works will constitute the improvement and delight of all generations. On the other side of the Atlantic, such names, not to specify those of living authors, are a- familiar as household words, not only among the learned, but among the masses of the people. These, by the blessing of Heaven, have generally received a common school education, and are able to read and to relish the standard works of your best authors. þÿ I delight in the reflection and the hope that the literary and scientific men of Great Britain

and the United States will constitute a perpetual bond of peace and friendship between the people of the two countries. Your men of this class belong to us, as our men of the same class belong to you. Wc have each a common property in both. happy influence Fhey cannot fail on to the exercise a mutual and most two nations. It has been the misfortune of both, that almost ever since the period of the American revolution, there has been a succession of disturbing and dangerous questions between the two governments. The irritation arising from these can always be allayed, and their unhappy consequences may, I trust, be always averted by the productions and common sympathy of the men at the head of the republic of letters. May the time never arrive when these men shall be arrayed against each other ! The consequences might then bo disastrous. þÿ Before resuming my seat, I must, in order to gratify my own feelings, express an unqualified approbation of the Literary Fund Society, and its most praise-worthy objects. It does not confine the relief which it bestows to British authors alone, but, in a spirit of genuine liberality, extends its benefits to those of other is nations. Genius, as has been justly observed, always sensitive ; and, therefore the bounty of Society is distributed in the most secret and delicate manner, so that the feelings of those who receive it are ppared from public observation. May this Society be always prosperous, and may it always be amply provided with the means of extending
its blessings and its benefits to a class of men tu whom mankind are so greatly indebted þÿ

Christiansted, St. Croix. FRIDAY, , JULY 20/4, 1S55. W k publish to-day a continuation of the verv important news brought by the last packet, connected with the War in the East. It was expected that under the command of Generals Simpson and Pelissier the Allied Armies would soon render glorious service to their respective countries, and vigorously redeem the check sustained by them in the late attack on the Malakoff Tower and Redan Batteries.

European Extracts. From the London Times. The despatches published in the Moniteur of I'riday, confirm in part the sinister rumours which had been in circulation for some days, and which commenced even before the events to which they related had occurred The Redan and the Malakhoff Forts were attacked on the 18th ; the troops penetrated to the latter, and partly occupied it, but they were unable to mainnumbers, and exhausted by their own impetu- by tain their position, overwhelmed probably osity \\ e learn, with the deepest pain, that

3 Ifs Q Hi ID 1£ a T It 3s the losses of the allied forces are believed to be greater than in any former action of the war. Sir John Campbell, Colonel Yea, of the 7th, Colonel Shadforth, of the 57th, and many other officers of distinguished gallantry, fell in our rauks, while the I' rench have lost three general officers and a vast number of men in all branches of the service. A rumour is afloat to the effect that another attack was made on the 19th, which also failed, but that on the 20th the troops returned to the struggle, and that after considerable loss the Redan and Malahkoff were at last taken. It is rumoured, likewise, that the Mamelon itself had been evacuated. The Malahkoff Fort is the key of Sebastopol ; it is of tremendous strength, and as might have been expeoted, the Russians defended it with the utmost desperation. The division of General Mayran (French) is said to have been the one most engaged, and that suffered the greatest loss. It is also stated that a despatch has been received in Paris, announcing the loss of an English general and several officers A private despatch from Varna says that Genl Pelissier had demanded reinforcements.

From the þÿ London þÿObserver. One thousand men per week are enlisting into our army. þÿ'J hisis at a time when we have literally no unemployed class, in any department of industry ; but on the contrary, labour is everywhere sought for, aud wages high. The fact evidences the warlike ardour, and the spirit of military enterprise, that animate the people of this country. But large as this voluntary recruitment is, it is still insufficient to supply the number of men voted by Parliament for the present strength of the army, and at the same time to make up for the constant drain of men which the war occasions. An additional inducement is, therefore, about to be offered in the shape of a boon to our soldiers, which, we have no doubt, will vastly stimulate and increase the enlistment. There have been great ameliorations made in the British þÿsoldier condition s of late years, and his comfort and improvement have been studiously promoted, but there was undoubtedly ground for the complaint that his pay was too low, compared with the general rewards of industry þÿ so low, indeed, as to operate as a discouragement to men leaving other occupations for the military life. We therefore receive the announcement made by Lord Panmure on Thursday night, in answer to a question of the Duke of Richmond, with great satisfaction. The pay of soldiers is henceforth to be doubled, whilst actually serving against an enemy. This will of course apply to the whole of the troops in the Crimea ; and the increase is moreover, to be retrospective, aud to take effect

from the day the army landed there. A distinction is to be made between the additional shilling a day granted to the private soldier, and his ordinary pay. It is intended, not to make an immediate money payment to the men, but to invest the increased amount to which they will be entitled under this arrangement in the regimental þÿsavings bank, where it will remain as an acculating fund at interest until the soldier receives his discharge, or is pensioned off, when it will be paid over to him for his own disposal. In case of the þÿowner death s in the service, the money will be given to his nearest relatives. This part of the arrangement, as to the investment of the additional pay, is obviously dictated by an anxious desire for the þÿsoldier sultimate benefit. The old rate of pay sufficed to provide the men with all neeessaries, and leave a trifle as surplus, though a small one ; and it is therefore naturally felt that the bonus would be better invested as a fund for enabling them to start in the world, on leaving the army, than be paid to them as ordinary wages, in which ease, in the majority of in-

stances, the money would almost necessarily be wastefully spent. It is adopted more as an experiment than as a permanent measure, and it will not be regarded as a definitive settlement, until the opinions of the soldiers themselves have been ascertained. In addition to this great boon to the English army Lord Panmure stated that his attention was still directed to the question of improved barrack accommodation. His lordship indicated some points in which changes, that have long been called for, were about to be carried into effect. Whilst this proper and commendable care is bestowed upon the rank and file of the army, we are glad to find that justice is to be done to the claims of the officers, with regard to the pensions awarded to the widows and children of those who lose their lives in the service. These allowances are to receive a material increase, the particulars of which are given iu a royal warrant just issued, and, in case of an officer dying unmarried, and leaving a widowed mother or unmarried sisters in circumstances to require it, a pension will be awarded to those relatives. This will go some way to meet the case recently put, of the hardship suffered by the relatives ol those officers who have purchased their commissions,' and died in the service, when the value of the commission is lost, lu both measures we are sure that the Government will have the hearty concurrence of the country.

New of the War. The news of the war is more than usually grave. We have indeed still to learn the particulars of our ill-success on the 18th, and are still without tidings of any further attempt ; but while we wait time wears on, and nature takes its course. Lord þÿRaglan iron s constitution has at length given way to a cause that has laid many a younger and stronger man low, and his lordship has, we are told, requested to be relieved of his command, in order to return home. General Simpson, wc believe, will succeed him in the command-in-chief. Captain Lyons, whose talents and enterprise marked him for the command of the expedition in the Sea of Azoff, in spite of his comparative youth, and who amply justified the wisdom of the choice, has died of his wound It appears that, in his anxiety to make a thorough reconnaissance of Kaffa, he approached so near to the port that, standing on the paddle-box of his ship, he received a rifle ball in his leg. He did not think much of it at the time, but the extreme heat, the excitement of the occasion, and probably also a degree of vexation at being thus unnecessarily disabled, checked the healing process, and deprived the service of the very promising officer to whom wc owe our very first naval success in this war.

Tlic Progress of ft nils. The grand distinction between the position of Russia and of the Western Powers at the present time is this þÿ the war imposes on us no sacrifices beyond the outlay of a certain sum of money þÿ which can be raised without difficulty by taxation or by credit þÿ and the loss of a certain number of troops, who volunteer to fight the battles of their country. Trade is untouched ; money is so abundant that the Bank of England has just reduced the rate of discount to what it was in September, 1853 ; and the struggle in which we arc engaged has roused, but not exhausted our military and naval energy. Compare this state of things with the condition of the Russian empire. Tier entire maritime commerce is at an end ; the Baltic ports arc sealed, and produce can only be brought down at a cost of about £20 a ton to Mcmcl and Konigsbcrg ; the shipping and warehouses of all the towns of the Sea of Azoff arc destroyed, and it is stated that 360 rigged vessels and 300 lighters have perished there in the last j few weeks ; even the salt required for curing the fish which forms a large portion of the sustenance of the common people can no longer be procured.

tions of the empire are carried on is withdrawn, and the mouths even of the Don and the Dniester are closed. In whatever manner the public service in Russia may be provided for, the cost of warlike operations of this magnitude must be enormous ; yet she has no power of materially increasing the taxation of the country or of raising a loan, at homo or abroad. In one sense the taxation is frightfully increased, and that is by the incessant levies throughout the empire of men who are as much the property of the landowner ot Russia as the negroes of a Virginian planter. Wo think that no less than five general levies of from 10 to 16 men per 1,000 souls have been made since the commencement of hostilities, and the rigour with which it is found necessary to execute them may be judged of from the terms of the last ukase, enacting that all exemptions from the conscription arc to be annulled, that m towns men are to be taken to the age of 37 years, and that even two sons arc to be taken, if required to complete the numbers of the levy The Russian army, as it existed two years ago, consisted of a body of well-disciplined soldiers,

a 'J. 0 ii & 1 SL T 31 3« the majority of whom had served for a long period of years, and had attained a high degree of military perfection. Tens of thousands of these men have perished, and their places are supplied by raw troops. Moreover, the ranks of the Russian army do not supply that intelligent and admirable class of men from which the non-commissioned officers of the British and French armies are formed. The Russian non-commissioned officer is trained, like his superiors, in the military schools, and the private can very seldom be raised to that rank ; hence the supply of these essential members of a regiment is limited, and the losses sustained in the field are not easily replaced. We infer from the latest accounts that, independent of the actual progress and success of the purely military operations against Sebastopol or on the Tchernaya, all the general causes which must affect tho termination of this contest are operating powerfully in favour of the Allies and against the Russians. Even the danger that the enemy might find means to throw large reinforcements into the peninsula is obviated by the destruction of the supplies on the east coast ; and, the larger the Russian army is in the interior, the less time can it remain in that position. If the Russian Cabinet hopes to rescue auv considerable part of that army from a very critical and embarrassing position we do not hesitate to assert that the þÿ strategical þÿreasons which led some time back to the evacuation of the Princi-

palities prescribe far more strongly the evacuation of the Crimea ; and, although it is always hazardous to anticipate any occurrence in the rapid vicissitudes of war, we should not be surprised to learn that Prince Gortschakoff and his generals had suddenly taken some very decided measure to save themselves from a capitulation. Sebastopol, it must be remembered, is defended not only by a garrison, but by an army. One successful movement of the allied forces may at any moment cut þÿoff that army altogether from its base of operations, while the defence of Sebastopol is now probably only a question of time, and the want of supplies will render it every day more difficult cither to prolong the resistance of the place or to provide for the safety of the army in the field.

Tlte Turkish Army in theCrimen. The proceedings of the Turkish army in the Crimen up to the present ha\2 not liecn very satisfactory. 25,000 men have liccn withdrawn from Eupatoria þÿ the best troops of the garrison, and fully capable of rendering important assistance in the operations of the siege, but their usefulness is hindered, or at least marred, l»y a feeling of dissatisfaction on Omar þÿPasha part s regarding his position. It is certainly pardonable for a man who for the last two years, has been exercising a sway not only over his own The capital by which the ordinary trading opera- i soldiers, but over the province occupied by his army, little short of absolute, to feel dissatisfied on finding that, the moment he passes from the north to the south side of Sebastopol, lie sinks from the position of a generalissimo into one 1 of no greater importance than that of a general of division. This failing has shown itself in a great deal of little bickerings with the French, which do not reflect the least credit on either party, although, considering the various weakness which mark the best characters, it is difficult to blame either one or the other. General Pelissicr demanded aid from the Turkish division under Osman Pasha, posted in advance near Inkerman, in the shape of a fatigue party to carry gabions, which was refused, and this was followed by a letter from Omar Pasha, in which he informed the French General that he went there simply to aid in the operations in the field, and by no
means in those of the siege, and that he would, from considerations regarding their health, at once withdraw his troops

from the Tchernaya. This was met by a curt reply, in which he was informed he might do as soon as he liked. The breach was healed by a personal interview, and the Turkish division remained in the trenches, where they have, up to the present, had fifty men put hors de combat. Omar þÿPasha s return to Eupatoria, even if his corps d'Armee remains behind, is still talked of, as matters do not yet seem to have been made quite pleasant. This shows in the strongest manner the evils of divided command. The mildest and best tempered men in the world could not always get on well together, situated as the varied allied generals are. Poor Omar Pasha is the most unfortunate of all, as he, in virtue of his being the leader of þÿ þÿbarbarian troops, has been compelled almost ever since the beginning of the war to act under advice þÿ now emanating from the French and now from the English þÿ and, therefore, must have been very effectually bewildered, until he threw the French overboard, and surrendered himself bodily to English influence. Since then there has never been much cordiality between him and the French, and, on the whole, he is much in the position of the old man and his ass.

A PEEP AT CROMSTADT. Nearing Tolboukin from t lie sea, the low island of Cronstadt, with all its terrors, gradually rises in patchy hummocks, and to the southward singular rocky excrescences appear dotted about between it and the main, backed by the tall masts of the liners; these, with the gilt steeple of the church, which sparkles many a mile, are the most prominent objects. By degrees the haze so prevalent in this gull, and which veils or distorts both nature and art, is gradually dispelled, and these rocky excrescences assume a more determined shape. To the extreme right the enormous square block of masonry, mounting some 150 guns, is Risbank, looking nothing the worse for the winter, an additional work being apparent on its southern side, and a corresponding Hanking battery on the main for its protection ; next comes Fort Alexander, looking like an ill-conditioned hayrick; shortly after þÿI eter I. and Cronslot become visible, the latter of which it would have been difficult to improve, with a couple of three deckers moored across the entrance of the passage, supported by numerous heavy paddle-steamers, apparently under the special protection of Fort Menschikoff, which, with the mole batteries, forms the last of the long line of forts on or near the south shore of the island, which is now one vast intrenched camp, encircled by detached earthworks, all furnished with the heaviest ordnance, and finished with that scrupulous nicety which we have þÿ to respect at Sebastopol. < Hi that Bono learnt

þÿJohnny had abandoned Silistria, and our enemy had never been taught the value of mud in that sanguinary siege ! These detached works are carried right across the island from abreast of Fort Alexander on its south side commencing at the spot marked þÿ Kesel þÿBattery in the old plans, and extending to the þÿgovernor s house on the north, on the town side of which another huge earthwork is being constructed, affimling daily employment to about 3,000 men. These detached works are admirably placed, having a gentle slope in front of them, Hanked by and flanking Fort Alexander on the south, and on the north protected by the shoals, submarine piling, and infernal machines. All the old works outside this line, as well as Alexander Fort, are apparently abandoned, and with judgment, for the defences of the island against a land attack are rendered more compact, and the chances of a successful landing, which last year was the most, or one of the most feasible operations, is now rendered hopeless. On the north side the barrier of submarine piling has been much improved and extended ; the means employed are large wooden caissons, some 25 feet square, which are first floated over the place they are intended to occupy, and then sunk with stones, and afterwards filled with the same material ; passages are left between many of these piles about 18 feet in width, for the egress of their gunboats, should the north side be menaced. A fort and battery have also been erected on Eisi-noss, to Hank any

attempt to force the barrier, which is also protected by a line of floating batteries, consisting of four liners, five frigates, and two corvettes, together with some 40 gunboats moored within it, the distance varying from 500 to 1 ,000 yards, and stretching from the island to the main, and which will now, therefore, prevent the possibility of passing round and attacking from the eastward. The other vulnerable point, and which was

3 tl\ Q lU > 2i SL A K it 3 most accessible to a naval attack last year þÿ the line of defences on the north side ot the town þÿ has also been much improved, and very heavy guns mounted. Were þÿone e s yes to be trusted in Russia any more than þÿone ears, they s have actually built 12 steam gun-boats; but, as only two have been seen under way, it which may fairly be surmised that the remainder are dummies, with a funnel and wood fire at the bottom of it, for by this time our friends must have perceived our gullibility, and acted accordingly, vide Kertcli. 1 would here notice that 17 of their largest ships are dismantled and lying in the basin, which serves to show their confidence in the means of defence. The infernal machines, to which they have, in a measure, confided the defence of the north side, are no longer the myth of last year. One of our small steamers, when reconnoitring the other day, with the French admiral and several captains on board, very nearly received its quietus. She exploded two of these machines, whether from contact or otherwise is uncertain, luckily in five fathoms water; as it was, the one exploding under her starboard bow fairly lifted her out of the water, bulging in the side before the paddlebox, and ripping off much copper þÿ at the same time throwing up a column of water alongside about 14 feet high. Had it happened in shoal water, or had the explosion taken place more directly under her, it would

þÿo Guunt, destroyed by Warner ofl Brighton. These machines, when seen from a þÿvessel s deck, have the appearance ot' huge cylinders moored under water, well below the surface, with a funnel rising from the centre to within a few feet of the same, and the probability is that violent contact causes explosion, though it is perfectly possible, and even probable, that they are fired by batteries from the shore (on the þÿvessel s identifying herselt with their positions), more particularly as neither þÿot the explosions which look place was under the bottoms, but .alongside, and consequently the amount of damage was small. The energies of our antagonist have been little h ss vigorous in the north than at Sebastopol, considering the winter, and it is no exaggeration to state that this year Cronstadt is twice as strong as last. Something, however, may yet be done; should it be deferred until next year, that will be impossible ; but the golden opportunity was lost last year, when Cronstadt was as unprepared to resist the combined fleet and 30,000 troops as Sebastopol was to resist the combined armies. A TRACIF.DY OF ERRORS. W ar is a tragedy of errors. Blunder encounters blunder and accident accident, and success is for those who, in this great conflict of stupidities, blunder the least. It requires some philosophy of this kind to console any one who watches attentively the manner in which we have addressed ourselves to the great struggle with Russia. We had two main difticulics to apprehend in our contest with the Czar the one, the shallow waters þÿ which we should have to navigate ; the other, the enormous power of the artillery which has been accumulated for so many years by a power whose whole end anil aim seems to have been to concentrate the energies of a vast empire j twixt on the multiplication of the means of

destruction. Both I liese difficulties have turned out at least as great as could be anticipated, arid to these two advantages, the one natural, the other artificial, what have we been able to oppose? We have made war in shallow seas with ships of immense size and draught of water, and have encountered earthworks with a fire would be very effective against stone walls, but which loses all its effect against that which absorbs and ingulfs, instead of offering a hard and compact resistance to shot. The consequence is, that the coast of the Baltic have suffered little from our attacks, and that when we attempted an operation in þÿship boats s we were met at the obscure village of Gamin Carleby with a severe and not very creditable check. The account of Cronstadt shows only too plainly how completely we have been disabled by the want of gunboats. East year Cronstadt was vulnerable on many points; this year it is almost inaccessible; next year it will be absolutely impregnable. Our scythe will not be sharp enough to mow till the time for mowing is over. While Cronstadt was a comparatively easy prize we could send no proper vessels to attack it ; when it became more difficult our preparations had increased, though by no means in equal proportion ; and we have no doubt that by the time the attack has become impossible we shall be very efficiently provided with means lor making one. East have been a similar case to the þÿ John year the north side of Cronstadt was exposed to a flotilla of sufficiently light

draught to navigate its waters, and by such a flotilla the batteries which defend the deep channel might have been taken in reverse ; this year the approach is closed by piles and caisons floated out to the spot required, and then sunk by being tilled with stones, and by additional forts and batteries. East year a landing on the island was possible; this year a series of works and batteries seems to forbid all ingress from the land side But this is not all. The resistance which the Russian earthworks presented to ns at Sebastopol, and the immense distance by which a proper respect for the tremendous batteries of Risbank, Alexander, Peter, Cronslot, and McnschikolV separates us from the Russian fleet, all inculcate as a lesson the absolute necessity of encountering such obstacles, if they arc to lie encountered at all, by a vertical fire of the very largest shells from mortars of the very heaviest description. þÿ Ibid.

We have the melancholy duty to record the painful loss which the Diocese of Dominica and the Catholic congregations of these Islands experiences, by the death of His Lordship the Most Noble and Right þÿRov d. Michael Monaghan, Bishop of Roseau, at the age of 42 years. The distressing event occurred at 2 þÿo clockp. m. on Saturday, the 14th instant, at the residence of the Reverend Abbe Georgetti, the incumbent minister The Reverend and highly respected object of this notice embarked from the Island of his Episcopal See, contrary to the wishes of the inhabitants, who witnessed the event with the deepest sorrow, and prayers for the return of Ilis Lordship, who contemplated to obtain, by a change of climate to Europe, and u visit to his native land, some relief from a severe attack of liver complaint, under which His Lordship unhappily labored The malady assuming a graver character, the medical advisers here, after various consultations, expressed the opiuion that any further progress of the voyage would he dangerous ; these conclusions have been verified, notwithstanding the skilful and zealous attendance of the medical attendants þÿ notwithstanding the delicate attentions which the hands of friends could minister, or the voice of sympathy bestow, the decrees of Goo are immutable ! Surrounded with the solemn insignia of that Church, of which be was the faithful representative and distinguished ornament þÿ in flic full career of a worthy Patriarch þÿ of piety, of benevolence and good.

\fter receiving all the Spiritual rites administered by Abbes Georgetti and Ryan, Ilis Lordship, in the prime of manhood, breathed his last sigh, apparently free fro-m pain, evincing, at the close of his exemplary ministry, the patient and Christian spirit, of an holy and pious life, worthy of that End, which was Peace ! O death ! where is thy sting ? O grave ! where is thy victory ? The body, which underwent, the modern process of the renowned Dr. Suquct, and prepared under the direction of Dr Duchassaing þÿ the un-

38 IT- 0 3t 0 -T X All 3. remitting medical attendant of Ilis Lordship þÿ was then arrayed ill the Sumptuous Tunic and Vestments of the Episcopacy, surrounded at the same time with the various insignias of that office, together with other accessories, displaying great taste and judgment ; after which the building was thrown open (on Saturday evening) for the admission of an immense concourse, consisting of Catholics and members of other persuasions, who hastened to testify' their sorrow and respect. Previous to the demise of His Lordship, the most zealous attendance was manifested by numbers of the Catholics, who daily offered their prayers to Heaven, for the recovery of the august invalid. On the painful result being announced, preparations commenced at the Church, and within a short period the interior, as well as exterior, of the sacred Edifice was appropriately fitted with the emblems of mourning, in honor and conformity with the exalted rank of the deceased. The flags of the vessels in port were immediately lowered on the announcement of the event. Throughout the day (Sunday) the extraordinary movement among the population, too well indicated the mournful interest generally entertained in regard to the sad event. A considerable while previous to 5 þÿo clock, the hour announced that the corpse would be removed from the residence of the minister to the Church, the whole of the Main Street presented a peculiar and thronged appearance, the inhabitants principally in deep mourning, and all well dressed,

gradually increasing in number, particularly on the announcement of the commencement of the religious ceremony, precursor of the removal of the body to be conveyed to Church. It would be superfluous to add that the elegant mansion, the Parsonage, where the body lay, it may be conjectured, was crowded to excess, as well as the Courts, and all the avenues leading to the building. At 5 þÿo clock the tolling of the bell, and the appearance of the Cross, was the signal of the removal of the body. TIIF COLONIAL COt XCIL! 1 he time approaches when we inav look forward, in anxious expectation, for the 3rd Session ot the Colonial Council The Elective District ot St. Thomas has refused to return any members to this body. How far they have acted correctly, in this respect, is a question which w< opine can scarcely be well defended. The Colonial Council is not a legislative body, having power to frame and pass laws, subject only to the sanction of the king ; it is simply a consultative body, furnishing Government with advice in respect to drafts of laws, which do not acquire legislative force until they have subsequently been properly weighed by His Majesty þÿ , Ministers and Diet. Whether the Colonics arc justified in consider mg themselves ripe for colonial legislation or self-government, we do not mean to discuss þÿ but wc may take the liberty to offer us our opinion, that the electors of St. Thomas ought not lo affix so much importance, as they do, to their being disproportionately represented in the Colonial Council. Oil questions regarding the welfare of St. Thomas, should the representatives of that Island even be in the minority, it does not necessarily follow that the advice or opinion of the majority becomes law. We have already seen that measures have been vetoed in consideration of the advice of a minority. Were this Council a legislative body, then perhaps the electors of that district might suffer through a disproportionate representation, and perhaps might be benefited by having a sepavate

Council. Wc arc, however, of the opiuion, that the open disrespect shewn to the Colonial Law. by the electors in St. Thomas, in absenting themselves from the Poll, will not prevent a Session of the Council beiug held this year ; and the Constituency of St. Thomas might find itself worse off for not being represented at all, than from being disproportionately so þÿ We arc sorry that an Institution yet in its infancy, as is the Colonial Council, should be found to work unsatisfactorily. But there arc other means of having grievances redressed than that

of sliewin" so much indifference. 'I lie better course, think, wc would have been to have returned siicli meinbcrs as would liuve directed their energies to making known the wants of their constituents, and in devising measures cal cnlatcd to fulfil their wishes.

Nothing important has occurred since my last flic bombardment, which was very brisk for some days, has greatly slackened. Our firing must have been extremely destructive, if we are to credit the reports of the numerous deserters. The General-in-Chief, it is said, has received orders to waste as little ammunition as possible and await large reinforcements, now on their way, to strike a decisive blow. It appears that lief army. The plan is to drive the enemy out we are going to operate against the Russian re- ; of the Crimea and occupy the country, after fortifying Perekop. The sudden breaking up of Government the Vienna Conferences has no doubt suggested this now plan of campaign, for the assault had been positively fixed for the 28th of April. During the bombardment the fire of the Russians was not so animated ns was expected, I was on duty in the trenches when it was most violent, and our losses in men were insignificant. Our batteries suffered little, while on the side of our attack two redoubts of the besieged near the ravine of the Caroeninp Bay, were completely

Q ai I'lSL A T S ' destroyed. General Pelissicr directs the siege operations with remarkable ability. On the left side we are established within a few yards of the Flagstaff Bastion. The English are to batter down the Redau and Malakhoff Tower, and we shall assist them in storming those formidable positions. The bold coup de main of General Pelissicr had dispirited the garrison of Sebastopol which repeatedly attempted to recover works so bravely captured and so heroically defended by our soldiers. The Russians left the field strewn with their dead. We however, sustained heavy casualties. A few days afterwards the Russians again came, at noon day and in impossing masses, to attempt a last effort to carry these works, and were beaten back with greater loss than on any of the former occasions. Their movement was perceived by one of our frigates, stationed at tho entrance ot the port of Sebastopol, and on receipt of the information the division of General Pate immediately took arms. The artillery and the troops guarding the trenches received timely notice, so that the enemy, when debouching in mass on the side of the Quarantine Fort and along the sea was exposed to a most murderous fire of musketry and artillery. The Russians fled in disorder, with the loss of 1,000 killed and wounded. These two affairs had so completely demoralized the garrison that we intended to avail ourselves of the circumstanco.so make an assault on the city, when contrary orders wore received. The second corps is shortly to commence operations on the banks
of the Tchcrnaya. Wo are awaiting the arrival of all our reinforcements. Most of the French divisions of the camp of Maslak and the Piedinontese army have joined þÿus.

A letter dated Hamborg, the 28th May, in the hulcpenda nee Beige , says: þÿ þÿ According to letters direct from Revel, no hostilities had been commenced against the town by the English fleet down to the 21st. Steamers kept constantly moving along the deserted coast without meeting a single Russian military or commercial vessel. The English corvette Basilisk, which entered Memel on the 24th, confirms this state of inaction, temporary no doubt, of Admiral Dundas. The Russian Generals had not yet thought propci to proclaim martial law in the provinces of Esthonia, Livonia, and Cour- Iand. They were waiting until the allies should have made some attack or effected a landing to recur to that severe measure of general security. All the Russian troops quartered in the interior of the three provinces had been ordered by the General-in-Ghief Sievcrs to march immediately l towards the coast Those who were quartered at a great distance in the interior are to travel in carts put into requisition by the Commissariat þÿ'I he coast from þÿl olangen to Libau, which continues to be blockaded by two English frigates of the flying Squadron of Commodore Watson, is guarded only by a pulk of Cossacks and three squadrons of Hussars, echelonncd as far as Windan, which would seem to indicate that the Russian Generals consider it difficult for the allies to maintain themselves in that flat country, should they land in that quarter. But beyond Windau the troops arc disposed in masses, and extend

. from Riga and Pernan along the coast of the gulf as far as Revel, and thence along the road to Cronstadt. The light cavalry belonging to the army of General Sic vers has been increased to 1 1 regiments. A letter from Cuxhaven states j that yesterday an English steamer conveyed from that port to Heligoland 105 men, enlisted in Hanover lor the foreign legion. You arc aware no doubt, that the Government of the latter kingdom, which is on the best possible terms with England, has not followed the example of the other German Governments, who severely prohibited in their dominions all enlistments for service in foreign countries. I have already told you that the police at Altona had closed a recruiting-office, and arrested 20 men on board a J small vessel about to sail for Heligoland. That vessel belongs to a proprietor of that English island, and consequently to a British subject, protected by the maritime laws of that nation. PEACE AND WAR. þÿ To be or not to be? þÿthat the s þÿquestion. Were England now to conclude a peace on disgraceful terms, the British public would soon open their eyes to the

unpleasant fact that they had lost caste in the world. Every Englishman would begin to be ashamed of himself, and no doubt we should have people insisting upon some summary way of wiping out disgrace and defeat. But this is not to he done. So no peace at present, till the objects of the war have been attained, unless we would lose the respect of our neighbours in Europe and our subjects in Asia. But it seems ridiculous to talk of a discreditable peace at the very time when we are in a better condition than ever for war. Now that the whole of the French force has sailed, and the Sardinian Contingent is on its way, the allies will soon have in the Crimea not less than 200,000 of the best soldiers in the world, ready to undertake , anything, and able to do it. They cannot and must not return without taking Sebastopol, unless they would show us on how llimsy a basis a great military reputation can rest. England cannot afford this downfall, nor can the Emperor of the French. His throne rests on opinion. lie represents his people. He is of their election ; he is their idol, their voice ; and, so long as he prospers, their pride. Should his legions return with nothing to show for their campaigns but an enormous bill of costs and list of killed and wounded, he will have to light a harder battle at home than his generals have been doing in the Crimea. So, also, will the Government of this country, which is on its trial, and which will not escape the fate of its predecessor,
unless it can point to some success and to some guarantee better than Russian words.

But there is not even safety for a nation such as ours when she once begins to recede, for when our tide no longer Hows it will begin to ebb. The battle wc are now fighting at Sebastopol we shall, before long, have to fight nearer home, and even at home, if we confess our incapacity for war. It has ever been the boast, and even comfort of this country, that whereas no other can be at war but its own territory is outraged, its own towns and villages destroyed, and its own streams stained with blood, our soil is sacred. Wc neither hear nor see the war others wage, and have it in our own power to choose our buttle- field. We have been rather apt to choose it a good way from home. This requires that we keep to the ground we have once chosen for the decision of our quarrel. But, in point of fact, one place is much the same as another in these days, and to be beaten in the Crimea is the same thing as to be beaten all over the world. There is no such thing as a mere geographical reputation, and a man may as well expect to enjoy a character for probity in one place, which he does not in another, as to have a military reputation restricted to certain longitudes. We have to secure not only the fear of an enemy that is distant, but the respect of an ally that is very near, and of neighbours that are also within reach. Even now, when we press Austria to take the side of honour and advantage, she taunts us with the smallness of our own contributions to the war, and tell us we are not in a condi-

tion to ask the aid of others while wc do so little for ourselves. This, at least, shows the spirit we have to deal with, and it is a spirit that will be ready enough to assume the aggressive should the occasion ever occcur. We It ave to teach not only Russia, but all Europe and the whole world to respect us þÿ not for our numbers, not for our home territory, not even for the number of men we can bring into the field, hut for our evident determination to light out, at every hazard and cost, the cause wc have once embraced þÿ London Observer, May 27.

Tin- cm War ! The war goes on swimmingly upon every point. Every day heralds a new success. Since the venue lias been changed from Vienna to Kertsch every body seems to breathe a fresher atmosphere, and the influence has reached even the House of Commons, in spite of the fog raised by Graham, Gladstone, Bright, and Co. It is impossible to overrate the advantages gained by the Allies in their thoroughly successful cxpediton to the Sea of Azoff. Very substantial gains of positions, territory, towns, forts, provision, and munitions of war have fallen into our hands, strengthening us and weakening the I enemy in the most vital points. But the moral eftect of the complete clearance effected in these waters is still more important. Our sailors are employed at length in the work they delight in, and our soldiers have obtained, in their easy victory, a most healthy, as well as a most commanding position Every day we may look forward to most interesting and stirring details of the progress and victory on every side most cheering þÿ to all, but especially so to those who never yielded to black and melancholy despair. There is already encamped in the pleasant valley of Tchernaya an allied force of 00,000 men ready to take the field, with every necessary þÿequipment a force capable of being doubled, without relaxing for a moment the attack, which is fast closing every day upon the town, the batteries, the ships, and the harbours of Sebastopol The London Gazette and the Paris Moniteur have

given us the details of the desperate and glorious victory achieved by the French on the nights of the 22d and 23d of May, in front of the important Flagstaff Battery, which lias been so often disputed, hut which now remains in the possession of our gallant Allies The news conveyed bv the Elcotric Telegraph, yesterday, of the victory of Thursday evening last, the fith instant, is more important still. The French at once drove the Russians from the Mainclon and the White Works on its right and front. Some people confuse these works with the White Tower, or the iMalakoff, of which they arc only the outworks. But their importance has been proved by the many struggles that have taken place for their possession. 'The Mamclon was erected to save the Malakoff Tower, which is the key of their position, on that side. The White Works arc more down towards the water on the Sapounc Mount, and command the Malakoff on that side. To carry both these works in broad daylight, in the

face of the Russian batteries, shows to what straits they must lie reduced by the tremendous fire so incessantly kept up. This could not be effected without much loss, which is known to fie serious, although not yet accurately ascertained. In fact, the operations were still going on, and the attack continued still nearer to the dockyard and arsenals on that side of the Military Harbour. Every hour intelligence of their further Operations is expected, and wc arc in constant expectation of being able to announce further successes in a Second Edition. þÿ London Observer, June 10.

Tlie Knssi.-ui System. 1 he system of the Russians seems to be to destroy rather than to capitulate ; and wc shall not he surprised to find that even at Sebastopol they are preparing to blow up the works thev can no longer hold. The loss already inflicted on the enemy by the Kertch expedition must be enormous, and, from the vast quantity of gunpowder and arms accumulated there, as well as from the state of the military hospitals, the town of Kertch seems to have been used for one of the depots of the Crimean army. As this town, which is a flourishing and well-built place of 12,000 inhabitants, is now in the power of the allies, we shall probably obtain more information than we have yet acquired as to the mode in which the war is carried on by the Russians, and the next despatches will he of the greatest interest both as respects the effect of these operations on the enemy and the ulterior movements of the army now under Sir George Brown and General Autemarre.

An Extraordinary Tic la I. The attention of the Paris Academy of Sciences was, some months since, directed to a discovery made by M. Sainte- Ciaire Deville, professor of chemistry at the Superior Normal School, in conjunction with M. Wohler, professor of chemistry at the university of Cottingen, of the metal called aluminium. The Emperor, on hearing of it, ordered that every encouragement should he given to utilise the discovery, and some manufactured specimens of this metal will appear at the exhibition. In a report made to the Emperor by the Minister of Public Instruction, proposing that the two abovenamed savans shall be promoted to the rank of officers in the Legion of Honour, as a reward for their scientific skill, we find the following: þÿ "When this extraordinary metal, light as glass, white and shining as silver, almost as unchangeable as gold, malleable and ductile in the same degree as these precious metals, strong as iron, and which is capable of being worked into any form by casting, by the hammer, and by the file; when this metal, which is found in abundance in the commonest clav, shall have taken its place in the domestic economy and the arts, no astonishment will be felt at the encouragement which your Majesty has given in order to render its extraction easy and less costly. Once more it will be admitted, that everything is connected in science, and that the same wonderful discovery of the decomposition of bodies by the galvanic pile, which procured for Davy the grand prize found-

ed by Napoleon I., has led to this not less wonderful discovery of the conversion of potters' clay into a metal which may rival gold and silver in its unchangeableness, and iron by its abundance on the very surface of the ground. A correspondent of the Ohio Farmer lias used a cheap and very durable paint for the exterior of brick dwellings, which has already stood several years, and is now quite as fresh as when first applied. It consists simply of lime-wash, with sulphate of zinc as a fixing ingredient. Any requisite shade is given by adding the colors used by house-painters. A clear and rich cream color may be obtained by applying yellow ochre to the common new brick; a livelier and warmer shade will be added by a little Venetian red. Burnt Sienna may likewise be used. This paint is far cheaper than oil paint, costs but little more than common whitewash and nothing will re-, move it but the severest friction. Grccu Tea. In Blackwood's Maguzine for January we find the following quotation from a work on the Tea Districts of China, by Robert Fortune. The statement, which, the author says, is vertabim from his note book þÿ he having noted down the process at the time þÿ may enable the drinkers of green tea, who have an arithme-

tical turn of mind, to estimate the number of pounds of blue paint they imbibe in the course of a year. Black teas are not coloured : " The superintendent of the workmen managed the colouring part of the process himself. Having procured a portion of Prussian blue, he threw it into a porcelain bowl, not unlike a chemist's mortar, and crushed it in a very fine powder. At the same time a quantity of gypsum was produced, and burned in the charcoal fires which were then roasting the teas. The object of this was to soften it, in order that it might be readily pounded into a very fine powder, in the same manner as the Prussian blue had been. The gypsum, had been taken out of the fire after a certain time had elapsed, readily crumbled down, and was reduced to powder in the mortar. These two substances, having been thus prepared, were then mixed together in the proportion of four parts of gypsum to three parts of Prussian blue, and formed a light blue powder, which was then ready for use. "This colouring matter was applied to the teas during the last process of roasting. Ahout five minutes before tea was removed from the pans þÿ the time being þÿ by stick the superintendent took a small regulated the burning a joss- of porcelain spoon, and with it he scatterd a portion of the colouring matter on the leaves in each pan. The workman then turned the leaves rapidly round with both hands in order that the colour might " be equally diffused. During this part of the operation the hands of the workmen were quite
blue. I could not help thinking, that if during the operation, their taste would have been corrected, and, I may be allowed to add. improved. It seems per-

fectly ridiculous that civilized people should prefer these dyed teas to those of a natural green. No wonder that the Chinese consider the natives of the west to be a race of ' barbarians.' " One day, an English gentleman in Shanghai, being in conversation with some Chinese from the green tea country, asked them what reasons they had for dying tea, and whether it would not be better without undergoing this process. They acknowledged that tea wa9 much better when prepared without having any such ingredients mixed with it, and they never drank dyed teas themselves ; but justly remarked that, as foreigners seemed to prefer having a mixture of Prussian blue and gypsum with their tea, to make it look uniform and pretty, and as these ingredients were cheap enough, the Chinese had no objection to supply them, especially as such teas always fetched a higher price. " I took some trouble to ascertain precisely the quantity of colouring matter used in the process of dying green teas, not certainly with the view of assisting others, either at home or abroad, in the art of colouring, but simply to show green tea drinkers in England, and one particularly in the United States of America, what quantity of Prussian blue and gypsum they imbibe in the course ol a year. To fourteen and a half pounds of tea were applied eight mace and two and a halt candareens of colouring matter, or rather more than an ounce. In every one hundred pounds of coloured green tea consumed in England or Ame-

Administrative Reform. Thl following interesting debate in the British House of Commons we clip from the news-letter of our St. Thomas contemporary : þÿ " Large meetings have been held in London and elsewhere, agitating the Administration Re-

form movement. In the House of Commons þÿ " Mr. Layard, in a long speech, brought forward his motion on the subject. It was to the effect that the House viewed, with deep concern, the state of the nation, and was of opinion, that the manner in which merit and efficiency had been sacrificed in public appointments, to party and family influences, had given rise to great misfortunes, and threatens to bring discredit upon the national character, and to involve the country in great disasters. In a speech which occupied nearly three hours, he reviewed the several departments in the army, navy, diplomacy, and the general civil service, citing cases in each in support of his assertions, and he concluded by an energetic call upon the House to adopt his resolution by the way of initiating an effective reform. " Mr. Tite seconded the motion. " Sir Stafford Northcote admitted that considerable evils prevailed in the system of civil service, but argued that they were the necessary consequences of our political system. Mr. Layard had proposed, however, neither a remedy nor a substitute, but he (Sir S Nortbcote) recommended the suggestions for examinations and promotions, which he and Sir C. Trevelvan had made in their report upon the civil service, to be carried out. " Mr. Leveson Gower complained of the absence of any definite practical object on the part of Administrative Reformers. He opposed the motion because it had a tendency to weaken the credit of the Government " Mr. Peacock preferred Sir E. Lyttou's

amendment to Mr. Layard's motion. He concluded by making a warm attack upon the Government. " Mr. Gladstone said he could neither support Mr. Layard's motion nor Sir E. Lytton's amendment. At the same time he highly approved of the attention which the public mind was giving to the subject, because he was couviueed that if this attention continued to receive this practical character, great benefit would be done to the Administrative Department. He described what had been done in the way of improving the civil service. In many cases the late changes would effectually include the system of nomination, whilst promotion would go by merit. The obstacle, however, was a belief in the public mind that promotion by seniority instead of by merit was the best, and the consequence was a low tone in the civil service. Considering the question in this light, he was in favor of men being introduced into these departments by merit, and recommended rigid examinations, and the system of superanuations also required amendment. " Sir E. B. Lytton then moved his amendment, which recommended to the earliest attention of the Government the necessity of a careful revision of our various official establishments, with a view to simplify and facilitate the transaction of public business, and, by instituting judicious tests of merit, as well as by removing obstructions to its fair promotion and legitimate demands, to secure to the service of the State the largest available proportion of the energy and in-

telligence " The Chancellor of the people. of the Exchequer said that Mr. Layard's motion, besides being a resolution for Administrative reform, was a motion involving a want of confidence in the Government, which, if carried, must lead to their resignation. It was the second motion of this kind within a fortnight, and the very executive were entitled to ask the representatives of the country whether that Parliament should afford them distinct support, or that motions of this kind should not be lightly brought forward. He stated why he could not assent to the motion, and denied all its allegations. " Lord Goderich then moved the adjournment of the debate, on which the House divided þÿ For Adjournment 240 Against it Majority for the motion þÿ 29 211 "

In consequence of a difference of opinion having arisen between General Caurobert and General della Marmora, General Pelissier had found it expedient to remove General Canrobert from the command of the expeditionary army on the banks of the Tchernaya, and to appoint in his place General Morris, one of the most distinguished of the Algerian commanders. The British steamer Pactolus, which sailed from Constantinople the 6th inst., arrived this morning, bringing 1 60 sick and wounded French soldiers. The British steamers Lady Jocelyn and City of Baltimore, from Constantinople 4th inst., arrived last night. They brought 280 sick and wounded. From the Boston Baity Advertiser. Steamer in Mistress. Steamship Benjamin Franklin, from St. Thomas 27th ult., for New York, put into Norfolk in distress on Wednesday last, leaking very badly. There were about thirty passengers on board. The B. F. commenced leaking on the 4th, and all the male passengers were compelled to work incessantly at the pumps in order to enable the ship to make the nearest port. At one time the water was eighteen inches above the furnaces, whist the best time made was not more than five knots per hour. The steampnmps being resorted to proved to be choked with cinders so as to be useless. Some of the crew were sick, and the ship was short-handed of firemen and coal-passers. She had been lying in the harbour of St. Thomas for eight months, and put to sea in poor condition, being obliged to lay by several times for repairs. These statements are made by a correspondent of the New York Tribune.

From Havana. The latest date from Havana, is May 31st. The news is not of particular importance. By royal charter, a bank of discount, deposit, exchange and issue, is to be established at Havana, with a capital of 13,000,000, and to go into operation as soon as the same is subscribed for. Its issues are to be predicated upon the capital paid in thereof the amount ; one half and one third to be in specie in the vaults; further issues may be made of bullion. Discounts of paper are to be made for three months only, and may be renewed after payment. Interest is to be allowed at the rate of 8 per cent, per annum. Bills of the bank are to lie of no less denomination than fifty dollars. The
charter seems to provide all needful restrictions for the protection of the people and its especial creditors by deposits. The expectation is universal that it will be of great commercial utility.

From the Grenada Chronicle, June 23. The commemoration of Queen Victoria's Accession to the Throne was observed on Wednesday by a royal salute from Fort George, tired by the ltoyal Volunteer Artillery Company, in a manner which reflects great credit on the whole Corps, the members of which are under the drill of Corporal John llobinson, II. A., stationed here for the purpose by the Communder-in Chief, at the requisition of the Lieut.-Governor. There is some talk of re-orgamzing the Grenada Troop of Light Dragoons ; but few have as yet been found to enrol. Of the old Troopers, who in 1832 numbered 30 or 40 only six remain, amongst them Lieut.-Colonel George Fraser, and Major Aird.« Rain, high wind, lightning and thunder have been rife during the past fortnight. On Sunday night it blew a perfect gale, and the claps of thunder were very severe. The roads are much washed and rutted, and in some places so clogged Willi landslides as to be impassable. This weather renders it impossible to the Planters to proceed with the fag-end of the current crop, but aids in the work of culture towards the next. Ground provisions are luxurant and promising. The island is free from sickness.

Hurry and Despatch. þÿ No two things differ more than hurry and despatch. Hurry is the mark of a weak mind ; despatch a strong one. A weak man in office, like a squirrel in a cage, is labouring incessantly, but to no purpose, and is in constant motion without getting on a jot Like a turnstile, ho is in every body's way, but stops nobody He talks a great deal, but says very little; looks into every thing, but sees nothing, and has a hundred irons in the fire, but none of them are hot ; or should one of them be hot ; he burns his fingers with it

The following is a description of the East Indian settlement proposed to be given in exchange : þÿ Chandernagore þÿ a maritime town in Hindostan, in the province of Bengal, belonging to the French, built on the west bank of the Hooghly river, 16 miles N. N. YV. of Calcutta, and in point of situation, in every respect superior to that city; latitude 22 deg. 4!)' North, longitude 38 deg. 26' East. In 181-1 it had a population of 41,000 and its revenue amounted to 32,256 rupees a year. Since that period, however,' both have probably diminished considerably ; for the author of "Sketches in India," sppaking of this place, says, " large lofty houses and warehouses, discolored, de- I caying, and half empty, speak of lofty speculations and disappointed hopes, the forsaken monastery completes the picture." The streets are straight and well paved, but now present a scene of nothing but solitude and desertion ; and the trade, formerly so flourishing, " has been reduced to a mere nothing. I saw," says Bishop lleber, " no boats loading or unloading at the quay, no porter with burdens in the streets, no carts, no market people,

and in fact, only a small native bazaar, and a few dismal looking European shops." There are some manufactures of Cotton cloths ; the commerce is chiefly in opium. The territory originally attached on this town, extended to two iniiesalong the river, and one mile inland : about two miles below Chanderagore, are the ruins of the superb house ; the country residenceof the former governor. |.\r. Ii08. General Pelissier. Of General Pelissier, it is not too much to say that no otlicer in the French army has a higher reputation, whether for valour, energy, oi ability. His arrival in the camp a short time ago was hailed as a good omen. There was at once a presentiment that lie was destined for the chief command. Very early in his military career Pelissier, when a young man in Paris (he is now only 44) got into some little trouble, in consequence of which he was sent to Africa, by way of punishment. There lie soon acquired the reputation of a fire-eater. It is narrated of him, that on one occasion being, sis chef de batlaillon, in command of a company of a punishment corps called the Zephyrs, lie attacked a mud fortress occupied by Arabs. His men in vain attempted to get over the wall. The Arabs kept a good lookout and repulsed every assault. Pelissier at length said to three or four men about him, þÿ Throw me over, 1 am sure the company will follow þÿme. His orders were executed. For two or three minutes he was alone in the þÿenemy position, s and in that space of time he received three or four wounds. Rut he had rightly judged the effect of his hardihood. The men followed him, and the place was taken. General Pelissicr has been much reflected upon for what has been, as I believe, very inappropriately termed the massacre of Dahra, in 1845. He was accused by the journals of the time of having cruelly and unnecessarily roasted to death a large number of Arabs, þÿ men, women, and children þÿ by lighting an enormous

fire at the mouth of a cavern to which they bad retreated. I am assured by many people that when all the circumstances are considered the reproach against him of having violated the laws of war is unjust. There were, in fact, hut very few women and children in the cavern, and General Pelissier did not know that there were any. He found that as he was moving his men from a position the Arabs continually sallied forth from the cavern and harrassed their rear. He lighted the fire in the hope of forcing the chiefs to come out and render themselves - prisoners, but unfortunately they were all stifled either from their own obstinacy, or from the fire taking more rapid effect than had been estimated. I really believe that the deed was nothing more than one of the stern necessities of war. It has, however given Pelissier the name of a man who is very much the reverse of chicken-hearted, and people chuckle at the idea that he is the man to roast the Russians in Sebastopol.

Extraordinary Scientific Discovery. þÿ A discovery has been made in Paris, by which any metallic poison, such as lead, mercury, or arsenic may be extracted from the system, by the potent agency of electricity. The modus operandi is as follows A metallic bath is insulated on glass legs and partially filled with acidulated water, to convey more readily the electrical currents. The patient lies upon a scat in the tub insulated entirely from the bath. When gold, silver, or mercury is in the system, nitre or hydrocholoric acids are employed. When lead is suspected, the acid used is sulphuric. This done, the negative pole of the battery is put in connexion with the bath, while the positive pole is in the hands of the patient. Now the work of purification commences. The electricity precipitates itself, hunts, digs, searches, and discovers every particle of metallic substance concealed in the most profound tissues, bones, nerves, and joints of the patient, resolves them into their primitive forms, and extracting them from the human organism, deposits them upon the side of the bath, where they can he seen with the naked eve.

Many of our clergy are doing it every week ; we wish there were yet more of them who | followed the same useful and holy enterprise ; but we are quite sure that the dull, formal preachers who are said to weary or drive away so many discontented auditors by their prosy sermons, would preach not a whit the better if they were to forsake their old manuscripts for Malthus, or exchange their concordances for Adam Smith þÿ þÿ s >- o þÿ RUSSIAN SISTERS OF MERCY.

The Berlin correspondent of the Times gives an interesting account of the Russian Sisters of Mercy engaged at Sebastopol Of the Sisters of Mercy who left St Petersburg for the Crimea, ninety-six in all, at least sixty-three are stationed in and about Sebastopol ; of the latt. r number, at least half are in the towns itself, and at the different surgeons' stations. The letters received in the capital from them, and those around them, pourtray in Carnage which the fire of the besiegers causes the Russians. It appears that the wounded arc for the most part removed to he north side of the ' fortress and thence to the interior ; but from the frequent want of means of trausport, and on the other hand, from the expediency of moving those j for the English 150 miles broad. The severely wounded, the numbers in the town become extremely unmanageable. The extreme distance from their sources of supply makes it impossible convey to to the troops, much loss to the sick, all the necessaries they require ; the article of which there was the least deficiency was i collision with the steamers. Lieutenant tea, so essential to the comfort of a Russian ; but of sugar there was a great lack, so that even the officers were obliged to bo allowanced. Leeches cost a silver rouble a-pieee. The descriptions of the scenes these pious females passed through are fearful. That of March 24th is more particularly mentioned, on which occasion six hundred wounded were brought in for treatment in twenty-four hours. From the number

of amputations and other serious operations, in which they assisted the surgeons, they frequently had to stand on a floor some inch or two deep in blood. The visit paid by two of the ladies, accompanied by a priest, to the Malakhoff Tower, and their celebrating divine service there, under 'he fire of the enemy, partakes of the romantic. After climbing the hill, and entering the fortress, where they find the soldiers and sailors assiduously occupied in returning the incessant fire of the enemy, they reach the tower, now destroyed, where the deceased Kornileff formerly had his quarters. After passing through a casement occupied dark corridor, with a row of by the sailors, they attain a long, deep, oaken columns on each nda. Here mass was celebrated ; the chants and other sacred songs were not omitted ; all the necessary paraphernalia was at hand, having been brought thither from a church that had been destroyed, and, after a sermon from the Pope, tbey carried the church vessels in procession round the bastion, with tapers in their hands, 'he enemy firing all tho time ! The Progress ol" the Submarine Telegraph. The American Telegraph Company expect to have telegraphic communications from Europe, via St. John's, Newfoundland, to New York, before the close of the season. The company is preparing to lay down, under the Atlantic, a submarine cable from St. John's to Newfoundland, for which purpose a contract has been made with some French and English operators to complete the same within three years. In 1858, it is said, London and New A'ork will communicate hourly by telegraph.

Wt record to-day in our columns another mstanoe of Suicide, committed by a prisoner Not long since one of these unfortunate men precipitated himself into a well, and was drowned. These occurrences suggest very forcibly to our minds the urgent want of moral and religious training in our prison discipline

3T, e lit <8> i£ A NT It 3. George Combe, in his work entitled " Criminal " Legislation ' An eye for an eye, and and Prison Discipline," a tooth for a tooth,' observes : þÿ called savage justice, and Johnson defines ' re- embodies the principle of revenge. This has been venge' to mean ' return of an injury,' and the wreaking of one's wrongs on him that inflicted them.' Another authority has said, ' Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do.good to them that hate you, any pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.' In a civilized country, criminals are the great enemies of society : indeed, when we are not engaged in foreign war, they are our only Corporeal foes. In dealing with them, then, on which of those maxims have we hitherto acted ? What success has attended our efforts r And which principle shall we follow iu future ?" An answer to these questions, as far as we in the treatment of our criminals are concerned, cannot be otherwise than that we merely puuish, but do not think of reforming them That class which supplies the greatest number of our prisoners is the one possessing the smallest degree of moral and religious training. Why wo have not a larger proportion, must simply be ascribed to their inherent natural good. It becomes then our duty, sinoe we cannot elevate the whole class, to try all the means in our power to reform thoso who, by violating the law, become dangerous to society. But as before observed, the idea of reformation does njt enter as a principle in our prison disci-

pline. Should a prisoner be incarcerated for years, the sound of a teacher's or minister's voice never enters his ears lie is abandoned by all save the jailer and driver. He is left in solitude, to meditate on the injustice which he, in his ignorance, fancies has been inflicted on hitn After the expiration of his term of imprisonment, he is allowed to go forth into the bosom of society, a more reckless and daring, but by no means a better man. The question, then, is how, during the period of confinement, shall these prisoners be fitted to re-enter society ? We can conceive of no difficulty iu the way of their receiving instruction from the Ministers of the Churches to which they are attached. It is a duty on their part which we consider a great neglect to have omitted. If any man calls loudly for the voice of truth and mercy, it is these men : and our christian Ministers should remember the words of their Divine Master, who said, " they that arc whole need not a physician but they that are sick." It cannot bo expected of us, to point out the time and place for such instruction ; we merely point to the want of it. And upon the principle that " a hint to the wise is sufficient," we leave it to be carried out hy those whoso province it is to make such arrangements

The Packet ! As we presumed would be the case, the splendid iron paddle-wheel steamer Atrato þÿ th» largest ship of the Royal Mail Company's fleet þÿ under the able command of Captain Woollet, arrived at St. Thomas on Monday morning last with the European Mails. Our letters and papers per packet Vigilant were landed here on Tuesday afternoon, after the issue of our sheet. Our exchanges from the Windward Islands have not come to hand, þÿ owing, no doubt, to the absence of the steamer Eagle when the packet left St. Thomas. We are indebted to "Willmer A" Smith's" of the 16th, for our principal extracts. The latest accounts from the Crimea are encouraging. The bombardment on the part of the English had again commenced, and the fire of the Russians was feeble. The Redan had been silenced, and our countrymen were enabled to push nearer their approaches to the place. The French were about to renew the bombardment of the Malakoff, and were engaged in erecting new batteries on the old Russian redoubts of Careening Bay. Mortars on a new system, the range of which was much greater thau those previously in use, were to be introduced, and great hopes were entertained of their success. These mortars, it is alleged, will reach the Russian line-of-batt!e ships and the Russian steamers, and prevent all future annoyance from that quarter In the course of a day or two we may expect to hear of some very decisive action. It appears that these instruments of destruction are placed in pairs, connected together by rope (in a the centre of which a float is attached), at a distance below the surface of the water varying from nine to twelve feet. Their apex points downwards, and they are moored by means of large stones at the bottom of the sea. Through holes bored in the centre of the stones a stout rope passes, which is firmly secured to a ring screwed into the apex of the machines. On the 21st ult., about noon, each vessel commenced sweeping for the infernal machines, and before night gathered in a capital harvest of them. The way þÿ which the sweeping is done is this: in Two boats take between them a long rope, which is sunk to the depth of ten or twelve feet by means of weights, and held suspended at that depth by lines attached to small casks, which float on the surface at intervals of forty or fifty yards; the boats then separate as far as the rope will allow, and pull in parallel lines until one of the casks stops behind, which tells them, as a float tells the angler, that they have caught something; the two boats then approach each other, keeping the rope taut, then haul it in carefully, and up comes the machine. Telegraph: Across tlie Atlantic. Two Companies have been formed, which propose lo act in concert in carrying out this great enterprise. The New York and Newfoundland Company arc to construct a line from St. John's across to Newfoundland and Cape Briton, to connect with the line from Halifax to New-York. This they hope to complete in the course of the year. The other, the Trans-Atlantic Company, are to carry it across the ocean, but are still undecided as to the choice of a route. To go directly across from Newfoundland to Ireland will require a continuous cable nearly 2000 miles long, while to go round by Greenland, Ireland, and the Faroe Islands to the North of Scotland, would require no submarine for any of its links more than 500 miles long. þÿ American Paper.

Adulteration of Port Wine. þÿ Some the Treasury and the Customs relative to the adulteration of port wine with " jerupiga" or " geropiga," and this was published on Thursday on the motion of Mr. Macartney, M. P. The correspondence was opened in February, 1849, by Mr. Johnston, the British Consul at Oporto, who wrote to Lord Palmerston on the subject of mixing port wine with "geropiga." It appears that "geropiga" is used in Portugal to give wines the appearance of possessing qualities which they really do not, þÿ or, in plain English, to "doctor" them. It would appear to be a villanous compound of elderberries, brown sugar, grape-juice, and brandy, every pipe of " geropiga" containing at least 35 imperial gallons of brandy, commonly upwards of 25 degrees above proof. In England Mr. Johnston believes that it is mixed with the harsher kinds of Spanish and Pontac wines and other "imitations" of wines. Tavern-keepers are said to employ it to mix with different beverages instead of spirits and sugar, and with great profit to themselves. Mr. Johnston submits that this compound might be properly considered as "sweetened spirits" and be subject to import duty as such. There is no export duty levied on it at Oporto, although on wines an impost is levied of 3/. 6s. per pipe. Mr. Johnston is convinced that if the export duty on wines were abolished in Portti gal, and the objects of the supervision of the trade limited to the prevention of the adulteration of wines and the punishment of the adulterators, a great

quantity of pure, good, and not heady wines of different kinds might be exported to England at moderate prices. Consul Johnston repeated his suggestions respecting "geropiga" in 1850 and 1853. and backed his statements by Portuguese official documents, clearly proving that "geropiga" was imported into Bristol "as wine," and used for adulteration, the worthy consul contending, on the strength of these disclosures, that it ought to be prohibited or saddled with a higher duty. It further appears that the Lords of the Treasury, in 1853, refused the application of a Mr. J. Norris to enter 10 pipes of "geropiga" on payment of the duty on wine, for this reason, þÿ that the strength of the compound (44 per cent, of proof, spirit) constituted it "sweetened spirits," as which Mr. Norris might enter the " geropiga" it he pleased, Afterwards, however, permission was accorded to Mr. Norris, by the Treasury, to blend the 10 pipes of " geropiga" with wine in bond, in proportions not exceeding 20 gallons to 100 gallons of wine. At length, after some communications between the Customhouse and the Treasury, their Lordships, on the 28th of June, 1853, directed that 33 per cent, should be the proper proportion to be allowed as the maximum quantity of proof spirit in wines, to be admitted to duty as such, and that all liquors imported beyond that strength charged 20s. a gallon as " sweetened should be deemed compounds, and spirits," time approved of " geropiga" being al- Their Lordships at the same
lowed to be mixed with wines in bond in the same proportions as brandy. þÿ London Paper
